Infant-Toddler Program IFSP Review — North Carolina

Family information and participation

This review concerns Nico Álvarez Soto, called Nico at home, born March 12, 2024. The meeting occurred on October 12, 2026, from 10:00 a.m. to 11:15 a.m., at the family’s apartment, 284 Lantern Finch Lane, Apartment 3B, Thornwell, North Carolina 27900, in Alder Ferry County. The child’s age was 2 years, 7 months. The record number is IT-26-01482, and the Medicaid number is 748203916Q. Spanish and English are used daily. The family requested an English document with verbal review in Spanish. Both parents participated and confirmed that the written priorities reflected their discussion.

Mother Mariela Soto and father Andrés Álvarez share caregiving and decision-making. Their preferred telephone numbers are 252-555-0146 and 252-555-0183, respectively. The family email is alvarez.soto.family@example.invalid. Mother requested text reminders before visits; father requested telephone contact for schedule changes. Sister Luz Álvarez Soto, age 6 years, lives in the home. Maternal grandmother Celia Soto provides care on two afternoons each week. Babysitter Tessa Bell provides occasional evening care. The family authorized routine coordination with these caregivers, limited to agreed communication strategies and scheduling. The parents requested separate permission before sharing assessment reports with extended relatives.

Service coordinator Ms. Elena Mercado, of Laurel Bend CDSA, facilitated the review. Her office is at 62 Meadowglass Court, Thornwell, North Carolina 27900. Her telephone number is 252-555-0124, and her email is elena.mercado@laurelbend.example.invalid. The office information page is https://laurelbend.example.invalid/families. I, Camila Ríos, a bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist employed by Two Rivers Pediatric Communication, completed the communication review and documented the plan in English. I conducted family interviews and play observations in both languages. The parents declined an additional interpreter because they could discuss the plan directly with me in their preferred language.

Mother stated, “I want him to tell us what he needs before he gets so upset. Mom works nights at Lantern Coast Linen Services as a laundry machine operator, so our mornings are quiet and sometimes rushed. I need something we can do while getting dressed, not another assignment.” Father stated, “I want to understand him when we play outside. I do not want him to feel that Spanish is wrong. He hears both languages, and we want him to keep both.” The parents identified requesting help, joining play, and communicating discomfort as their highest priorities. They also wanted fewer communication breakdowns during transitions.

The parents described strengths that they want services to build upon. Nico notices changes in familiar songs, brings books to adults, imitates practical actions, and enjoys making toy animals sleep. He checks an adult’s face when something surprising happens. He usually seeks his sister before trying a new game. Mother said, “He knows what everyone likes. He brings his sister the purple cup and brings Grandma her sweater.” The family values shared meals, Spanish songs, and visits with relatives. They prefer practical coaching with demonstration, time to try the strategy, and brief feedback. They do not want worksheets or corrections of every spoken word.

Daily routines and community supports

On weekdays, father begins breakfast around 7:15 a.m. while mother returns from work. Nico usually chooses between oatmeal and toast by reaching or pulling an adult toward the cupboard. When an adult waits without offering support, he may cry or leave the table. During observation, a choice between two visible foods supported a point followed by "pan". Mother responded to the request immediately and added a short phrase. The family agreed that breakfast offers a useful practice opportunity, but food will remain available without requiring speech. Adults will accept pointing, gestures, signs, pictures, and spoken attempts.

Dressing occurs after breakfast. Nico likes selecting socks but resists having a shirt pulled over his head. Father reported that the child sometimes says "no", pushes the shirt away, and then accepts help when the adult describes the next step. The family will offer a pause and model "help", "ayuda", or "wait". Bath time is enjoyable when the same cup and towel are available. Mother wants a clear way for the child to indicate that the water feels uncomfortable. Adults will model a simple gesture and the words "hot" and "cold"] during safe, ordinary comparisons.

At Little Lantern Early Learning Center, lead teacher Ms. Janelle Pike and classroom assistant Mr. Owen Reed reported that Nico watches other children closely and joins familiar movement songs. Classmates Maya Chen and Elias Brooks often invite him to the block area. He may take a desired block without signaling to its holder. Staff currently support exchanges by positioning themselves nearby, labeling the action, and offering a gesture for taking a turn. The parents approved a classroom observation focused on participation in play and transitions. Staff requested strategies that fit their existing routines and can be used consistently during busy periods.

Weekend visits include cousins Alina Soto and Teo Soto, who enjoy pretend cooking with Nico. Their aunt Verónica Soto supervises these visits. The family’s dog, Miso, frequently approaches the play area, and the child sometimes calls "doggie". Adults will keep pet interaction supervised and use it only when everyone is comfortable. Sister Luz likes being a play partner but will not be responsible for therapy practice or interpreting unclear speech. Babysitter Tessa asked for a short description of helpful responses. The parents agreed that she can use the same choices, pauses, and acknowledgment of gestures used at home.

The family receives nutrition support through Alder Ferry Family Nutrition WIC and transportation assistance through Alder Ferry Community Access Services. Thornwell Smart Beginnings provided a lending-library referral. The parents reported no current involvement with Alder Ferry Family Support DSS. Pediatric care is provided by Dr. Priya Mehta at Meadow Harbor Children’s Clinic. Occupational therapist Rowan Ellis, with Growing Steps Pediatric Therapy, consults on dressing participation. These agencies have separate roles. The coordinator will confirm existing releases before exchanging information. The family identified transportation reliability and mother’s work schedule as practical barriers, rather than lack of interest in services.

Assessment and progress

The initial communication evaluation occurred on April 14, 2026. The current review combines caregiver report, classroom information, direct observation on October 5, 2026, and assessment findings. The Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale showed consistent receptive skills within the 18–21-month range and expressive skills within the 15–18-month range, with scattered higher skills. These developmental descriptions are criterion-referenced findings, not standard scores. Skills observed in either language contributed to the description. The review did not interpret bilingual exposure as a cause of delay. The child’s communication needs appeared across languages and routines, including situations with familiar speakers and familiar materials.

The earlier multidisciplinary assessment included the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition, with a language composite standard score 78 and 7th percentile. The motor report used the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales, Third Edition, with a gross motor index standard score 94 and 34th percentile. These results describe the assessment conditions and do not replace observations of daily participation. The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition was considered but not administered because the available naming sample was insufficient for a useful standardized interpretation. No articulation standard score was assigned. Speech sound observations remain descriptive.

During a supported play sample, Nico communicated for requesting, rejecting, commenting, and seeking assistance. He used gestures with spoken attempts in 8/10 observed opportunities when adults provided mod cues. He independently initiated communication in 4/10 opportunities. Approximately 60% of the sampled messages were understood by a familiar listener with contextual support. Productions included "ma agua", "open", "mío", and "uh-oh". The sample contained [w] substitutions for some intended sounds; the observed production [w] and target phoneme /k/ were recorded descriptively. A SALT notation of [EW] identified an extraneous word in one sample utterance. These observations do not establish a separate speech sound diagnosis.

The prior outcome addressed requesting during meals and play. Family logs showed progress from mainly pulling an adult’s hand to combining a gesture with a word in several familiar routines. Performance varied when the child was tired or an item was out of sight. The team judged the outcome partially achieved and agreed to extend it into transitions and shared play. Mother stated, “We can see the difference, but he still needs us to understand the first little signal.” The parents requested that adults respond early to these signals. The next review will consider both successful messages and the support needed to produce them.

Outcomes, strategies, and services

Outcome one: By January 12, 2027, Nico will communicate a choice, request, or request for help during breakfast, dressing, and play in 8/10 naturally occurring opportunities across two consecutive weeks, using any effective combination of gestures, pictures, signs, or words, with no more than min cues. The family will select one manageable opportunity within each routine. Adults will position choices where the child can see them, model a short message once, and allow a comfortable pause. They will acknowledge the first meaningful signal and provide the requested assistance when possible. Success will reflect communication that works, including Spanish and English messages.

For this outcome, the speech-language pathologist will coach the parents through demonstration, guided practice, and reflection. Models may include "help me", "más agua", and "open please", adjusted to the child’s current attempts. Adults will expand a message without requiring repetition. If the child becomes distressed, the adult will address the immediate need and return to practice later. Mother and father will record a brief example on three days each week, noting the routine, message, and support. The clinician will review these examples during visits and compare performance across caregivers. The family may use spoken notes instead of written logs when that fits their schedule.

Outcome two: By January 12, 2027, Nico will participate in a shared play sequence with another child for at least 3 reciprocal turns in 4/5 opportunities across home and daycare routines, with min cues. Adults will begin with familiar activities, such as rolling a ball, feeding a toy animal, or adding blocks to a tower. Teachers will model "my turn", "your turn", or a matching gesture. Classmate Maya may participate when she chooses, and cousin Teo may join during family visits. Other children will remain play partners with their own choices and interests.

The team will define a reciprocal turn as an action or message that responds to the partner and allows the interaction to continue. Taking an object without responding will not count as a reciprocal turn. Adults will reduce language demands when the activity becomes difficult and restore an enjoyable rhythm before adding another model. Classroom staff will record one brief example weekly. The clinician will compare classroom reports with family examples and observe at least one group routine before the next review. The team will also note whether the child seeks a partner independently. Longer play will be encouraged when enjoyable, without making duration the only measure of success.

Outcome three: By January 12, 2027, Nico will signal discomfort or a need for a break during dressing, cleanup, and classroom transitions in 4/5 observed opportunities across two weeks, with min cues. Accepted messages include a gesture, picture selection, or productions such as "stop", "break", and "no más". Adults will introduce the message when the child is calm, demonstrate its effect, and respond consistently when it occurs. They will provide a brief preview before transitions and offer a manageable next step. The occupational therapist will contribute suggestions for dressing. The speech-language pathologist will focus on making the child’s message understandable to different caregivers.

Speech-language services will continue from October 19, 2026, through January 11, 2027, once weekly for 45 minutes in the home, with a classroom visit replacing a home visit when agreed. The usual appointment begins at 9:30 a.m. on Mondays. Service coordination will continue monthly and as needed through January 12, 2027. Occupational therapy consultation is planned monthly for 30 minutes, beginning October 22, 2026. Speech-language billing will use CPT 92507, with ICD-10 F80.2 documented for mixed receptive-expressive language disorder. Authorization SLP-26-730418 covers the listed communication service period. The coordinator will confirm payer approval before any change requiring additional authorization.

The family selected familiar settings because the outcomes concern communication during daily activities. The clinician will provide coaching within those activities and adapt visit timing when mother’s sleep schedule changes. The parents gave consent for the listed services and approved sharing this plan with the named daycare staff and treating providers. The coordinator will arrange the next review for January 12, 2027, at 10:00 a.m.. Transition planning will begin before the child’s third birthday on March 12, 2027. The family received procedural safeguards in English and Spanish. The review ended with agreement on the outcomes, strategies, service schedule, and methods for checking progress.

IFSP REVIEW — FICTIONAL TEST RECORD

Review date: October 6, 2026. Initial IFSP: April 6, 2026. Review period: April 7, 2026 through October 6, 2026. Next review: April 6, 2027. Child: Nico Esteban Varela, called Nico. DOB: June 6, 2024. Chronological age: 2;4. Record ID: NCITP-F482619. Medicaid ID: 583027164K. Visit completed in home w/ CG consent. This fictional record documents functional communication, participation, and family-selected supports. All identifying details, observations, and results are invented for testing.

FAMILY INFORMATION

Pt lives w/ mom Elena Varela, dad Tomás Varela, and sister Marisol Varela, age 6;1. Home: 284 Willow Lantern Lane, Bramble Cove, North Carolina 27864, Lantern County. Mailing address same. Mom's phone: 252-555-0146. Dad's phone: 252-555-0183. Family email: elena.varela@example.com. Preferred contact is text before calls. Spanish and English used daily; CGs request English documentation and Spanish discussion of unfamiliar terms. No language change requested. Family identifies shared meals, sibling play, and church visits as valued routines.

Mom works nights at Moonridge Linen Works as a packing-line operator, approx 10:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m.. Dad works variable shifts as a maintenance helper at Copper Finch Apartments. Maternal grandmother Rosa Mendieta provides care during overlapping shifts. Aunt Lidia Mendieta provides backup transportation. Babysitter Cora Bellamy covers occasional appointments. Family dog Mango remains behind a gate during floor play. CGs report transportation and changing work shifts affect attendance more than willingness to participate.

TEAM AND AGENCIES

Service coordinator: Keisha Rowan, Lantern County CDSA, office at 610 Meadowglass Avenue, Bramble Cove, North Carolina 27864. Office phone: 252-555-0108. Coordinator email: keisha.rowan@example.org. Family resource website: https://example.org/lantern-cdsa. Bilingual pediatric SLP: Isabel Cordero, MA, CCC-SLP, employed by Little Lantern Speech Services. Spanish interpreter Mateo Rivas attended by telephone for service coordination and consent discussion. SLP provided direct bilingual coaching; interpreter supported agency language outside the therapy discussion.

Other providers: OT Priya Halden addresses utensil use and sensory participation; PT Owen Serrano addresses transitions and safe mobility. Pediatrician Dr. Mira Denslow practices at Bramble Cove Children's Clinic. Community supports include Lantern County DSS, Bramble Cove WIC, Lantern County Smart Start, and Meadowglass Early Head Start. Family reports active nutrition visits, pending transportation assistance, and completed developmental playgroup enrollment. Coordinator will verify referral status w/ signed releases; reported enrollment does not establish completed agency intake.

FAMILY CONCERNS AND PRIORITIES

Mom stated, “I want Nico to tell us what he needs before he cries. When I come home tired, I cannot guess every sound.” Dad stated, “We want him to ask for help in either language. We do not want him to lose Spanish.” Grandmother Rosa Mendieta stated, “Meals are harder when the spoon falls. He pushes everything away, and I need a simple way to help him start again.”

CG priorities: easier requests at meals, fewer communication-related disruptions during dressing, and participation in peer play. Mom stated, “Please show us things we can do while cooking or getting shoes on. Extra homework will not happen every night.” Family selected brief practice embedded in existing routines. CGs prefer pictures, gestures, and spoken models used together. Family declines a separate daily drill schedule. SLP will coach adults to notice communication attempts and respond consistently.

DAILY ROUTINES

Wake-up occurs approx 7:15 a.m.. Dad offers breakfast and two choices before dressing. Pt points, reaches, and sometimes vocalizes; adults often anticipate needs b/c mornings feel rushed. During breakfast observation, pt requested a refill using "agua" following mod cues. At dressing, pt handed dad a shoe but did not independently request assistance. SLP modeled "help" and "ayuda", paired w/ an open-hand gesture. Dad practiced waiting briefly before assisting.

Lunch w/ grandmother occurs approx 12:15 p.m., followed by quiet play and nap. Evening meal occurs approx 6:00 p.m.. Sister Marisol enjoys pretend cooking w/ pt but sometimes speaks for him. CG will invite sibling to offer a choice, then wait. Bath, pajamas, and books follow supper. Pt enjoys animal pictures and imitates sounds during predictable pauses. Family will keep favorite books accessible and use repeated phrases during familiar bedtime routines.

COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION

Pt attends Little Acorn Landing two mornings weekly. Teacher Ms. Dana Quill and classroom assistant Mr. Elias Merren report easier transitions w/ a picture schedule. Peers Avery Moss and Tessa Bloom join block play; pt watches, copies actions, and occasionally takes a toy without signaling. CG permission covers exchange of routine-based strategies. Neighborhood volunteer Nolan Reed provides transportation to playgroup when available. Family requested that volunteers receive scheduling information only.

ASSESSMENT AND PROGRESS

Review used CG interview, bilingual play observation, and prior Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) documentation. Prior English administration listed Auditory Comprehension standard score 78, Expressive Communication standard score 74, and Total Language standard score 75. These fictional scores describe that administration only. English scores do not represent pt's total bilingual ability. Current decisions emphasize participation across languages, CG report, and observed learning w/ support. No new standardized score generated at review.

Across snack and play, pt communicated intentionally in 8/10 opportunities w/ gesture, picture, word, or combined forms. Spoken productions included "more agua", "go", and "mama help". Independent requests occurred in 40% of sampled opportunities; requests increased w/ mod cues. Informal speech sample showed variable final consonants and emerging /k/. One approximation contained [w] for a target liquid. SALT notation included [EW]. These observations guide modeling; no isolated articulation goal added.

OUTCOME 1 — REQUESTS DURING MEALS

By January 6, 2027, Nico will request food, drink, more, or help during two daily meal routines in 8/10 opportunities across three CG logs. Any functional mode counts. Strategies: position preferred items within view; offer two real choices; pause; model "more", "más", "water", or "agua"; accept approximations promptly. Begin w/ mod cues, then reduce to min cues as participation improves. Do not withhold necessary food or drink. SLP reviews logs and coaches one manageable adjustment weekly.

OUTCOME 2 — HELP AND TRANSITIONS

By February 6, 2027, pt will communicate help, stop, or finished during dressing and cleanup in 4/5 opportunities w/ min cues, across two weeks. Adults will use the same gesture and picture in both languages. Pair "help", "ayuda", "stop", and "all done" w/ immediate responses. OT will adapt clothing setup; PT will review stable seating. CG will record successful attempts and context. Crying remains a communication signal; adults provide comfort and offer an accessible alternative.

OUTCOME 3 — SHARED PLAY

By March 6, 2027, pt will complete three reciprocal play turns w/ an adult, sibling, or peer during 80% of observed opportunities across three sessions. Strategies: follow pt's interest, copy an action, introduce one simple variation, and pause. Model "my turn" and "your turn". Classroom staff will use familiar blocks and pretend food. Accept gaze, gesture, picture, or words as participation. SLP and CG will compare home and classroom examples before increasing task demands.

SERVICES AND FOLLOW-UP

SLP: weekly home visit, 45 minutes, October 12, 2026 through April 5, 2027; CPT 92507, ICD-10 F80.2. OT: twice monthly, 45 minutes, same dates. PT: monthly, 30 minutes, same dates. Service coordination: monthly contact plus referral follow-up as needed. Scheduling window: Mondays at 9:30 a.m.. CGs reviewed options and agreed to these fictional service entries. Coordinator will document agency replies, confirm transportation needs, and distribute the review to authorized recipients. Family received the plan in English w/ Spanish verbal review. No new medical findings reported. Next contact: October 12, 2026. Prepared and electronically signed by Isabel Cordero, bilingual pediatric SLP.

Review date: October 8, 2026. Child: Nicolás Vega Solís, called Nico; DOB June 8, 2024; age 2;4. Home: 184 Willowglass Lane, Bellpine, North Carolina 27998, Cedarfen County. Strengths include social interest, shared enjoyment, imitation during songs, and consistent caregiver participation. Family can practice strategies during meals, bath, dressing, and play without adding separate drill sessions. Mother identified breakfast as the first practice routine because materials and choices are predictable. Grandmother prefers picture choices near the refrigerator. Father prefers evening play and cleanup.

Progress since initial IFSP dated September 25, 2026: caregivers report fewer guesses during snack and more intentional pointing. Direct comparison is limited by the short interval and different activities. Current independent requesting baseline remains 3/10. Priorities remain unchanged. No regression reported. Sleep disruption and changing work shifts may reduce practice consistency. Coordinator will help align home and daycare strategies. Parents understand that progress will be judged through participation and communication across routines.

P:

Continue IFSP period September 25, 2026–March 24, 2027. Reviewed service plan effective October 12, 2026. Speech-language intervention: once weekly, 45 minutes, individual home visit with caregiver coaching; bilingual SLP responsible. Daycare consultation: once monthly, 20 minutes, with parent permission and teacher participation. Service coordination: monthly contact and additional contact for referrals or schedule barriers. No new equipment requested.

Outcome 1: By January 8, 2027, child will communicate a need during breakfast and snack using a word, sign, gesture, or picture in 8/10 opportunities across three caregiver logs, with min cues. Baseline 3/10 independently. Strategies: place desired items in view, provide two choices, pause, acknowledge all intentional communication, and model a short message in the language used during that interaction. Never withhold essential food or drink to obtain speech.

Outcome 2: By January 8, 2027, child will join a familiar adult or peer for 4/5 reciprocal turns across three play observations with min cues. Strategies: follow child’s interest, duplicate play materials, model giving and waiting, and use simple action words. Teacher will support brief block and ball routines. Caregivers will avoid requiring repetition before allowing participation.

Outcome 3: By February 12, 2027, child will use two meaningful communication elements, including words with gestures, in 6/10 daily opportunities across two routines with mod cues. Baseline 2/10 with max cues. Targets include "más pan", "mamá ven", and "more bubbles". Strategies: expand one element to two, accept approximations, repeat useful models, and avoid correcting every speech sound. Score Spanish and English messages equally when meaning meets the outcome.

Outcome 4: By February 12, 2027, child will complete cleanup and dressing transitions with a functional help or finished message in 4/5 opportunities with min cues. Strategies: show a two-step picture sequence, give one direction, wait, and offer help. Family will record successful transitions and the support needed. SLP will review logs during visits.

Coordinator will obtain audiology results after the scheduled visit, confirm transportation needs, and coordinate agency updates under current releases. Early education transition planning begins before age 3 years. Potential receiving program: Willowglass Preschool Learning Center; enrollment and eligibility are pending. Family resource page: https://bellpine-family-support.example/resources. Coordinator will document each referral response and unresolved barrier.

Next SLP visit: October 15, 2026, 9:15 a.m.. Next coordinator contact: November 5, 2026. Next formal IFSP review: January 8, 2027. Billing reference: CPT 92507. Parents reviewed strategies through teach-back and agreed with priorities, frequency, and locations. Written English copy supplied; Spanish verbal explanation completed. Clinician signature: Daniela Ríos, MA, CCC-SLP; signed October 8, 2026, 11:20 a.m..

NC Infant-Toddler IFSP Review / FICTIONAL TEST RECORD

Review date: October 8, 2026. Meeting: 9:15 a.m.–10:35 a.m., family home. Record: NCIT-FIC-004821. Review period: April 8, 2026 through October 8, 2026. All people, contacts, organizations, events, and clinical findings below are synthetic.

1. FAMILY INFORMATION

Pt: Nico del Río-Santos, called Nico at home. DOB: June 8, 2024. Chronological age: 2;4. Medicaid member ID: 900000014Z. Household address: 418 Juniper Lantern Way, Apt. 3B, Alderhaven, NC 27000, Hazelmere County.

Mother: Elena de la Cruz, preferred contact, (cell) (919) 555-0147; email elena.delacruz@example.invalid. Father: Tomás Vega-Ruiz, cell 919-555-0162. Parents share daily care and decision-making. Sibling: Luz Vega-Ruiz, age 6 years, attends Juniper Lantern Elementary.

Maternal aunt Hope de la Cruz provides backup care on rotating afternoons. Maternal grandmother Inés del Río joins occasional video calls from Mexico; phone +52 55 0000 0186. Household pet: dog Miga. Family reports stable housing, reliable utilities, and access to food. Transportation varies w/ work schedules; CG prefers home visits whenever possible.

2. TEAM, CONTACTS, AND PARTICIPATION

Service coordinator: Mara Fenwick, Juniper Bend Children’s Developmental Services Agency, office 919.555.0128, fax (919) 555-0196. Office: 72 Fern Compass Court, Suite 206, Alderhaven, NC 27000. Agency portal: https://juniperbend-cdsa.example.invalid.

Review authored by Iris Maren-Quill, bilingual pediatric SLP, employed by Riverglass Pediatric Communication PLLC. Clinician callback: +1 919 555 0184. Professional email: iris.marenquill@riverglass.example.invalid. Pediatrician: Dr. Devon Wrenfield, Alderhaven Children’s Pavilion.

Present: both parents, SC, and SLP. Aunt participated by phone for approx 15 minutes. Parents selected English for this written review and Spanish for most discussion. SLP interpreted her own clinical explanations; no separate interpreter attended. Team checked understanding through CG teach-back. Parents received a translated verbal summary and requested copies by secure portal. SC confirmed contact preferences directly during meeting.

3. FAMILY CONCERNS, IN THE FAMILY’S OWN WORDS

Mother Elena de la Cruz stated: “I know what he wants most days, but other people guess. When they guess wrong, he cries and pulls my hand. I want him to ask before he gets upset.”

Father Tomás Vega-Ruiz stated: “At breakfast he points to everything. I want us to slow down and let him try. I do not want speaking to feel like a test.”

Regarding daycare, mother stated: “I want him to tell the teacher when he needs help. He should have a way to say he is finished, even if the word is not clear.”

Aunt Hope de la Cruz stated: “He talks more when we sing or feed the dog. I need the same pictures they use at home.”

Family’s top priorities: easier requests during meals; fewer communication breakdowns during transitions; participation w/ peers; continued Spanish use w/ relatives. Parents do not want English practice to replace Spanish. Both agreed that gestures, pictures, and speech can support the same outcome.

4. DAILY ROUTINES AND FAMILY RESOURCES

Wake-up occurs approx 6:45 a.m.. Father handles dressing and breakfast before leaving for Copper Finch Fixture Works. Mother works variable shifts at Willow Thread Market. CG schedules change weekly; SC should text before calling.

Breakfast offers frequent requests for utensils, milk, and preferred fruit. Pt currently reaches, points, or brings an empty cup. CG often anticipates needs b/c the morning feels rushed. Dressing is easier when clothing choices remain visible.

Evening meal occurs approx 6:00 p.m.. Bath, book, and quiet play follow. Bedtime is approx 8:15 p.m.. Sibling Luz Vega-Ruiz enjoys shared books but sometimes answers for pt. Parents will coach sibling to pause.

Family strengths include predictable evening routines, strong shared attention during songs, nearby relatives, and willingness to practice briefly. CG prefers strategies embedded in ordinary activities; worksheets have not fit family routines.

5. DAYCARE AND COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION

Pt attends Little Lantern Grove Early Learning on three weekdays, usually 8:00 a.m.–3:30 p.m.. Lead teacher: Ms. Ada Lopez. Classroom is called “Ms. Lopez’s room.” Assistant: Benna Vale. Parent consent permits SC and SLP to exchange relevant routine information w/ these staff.

Classmates Milo Crest and Anya Bellweather often play beside pt at the water table. Staff report pt watches peers, copies pouring actions, and sometimes offers a cup. When materials disappear, pt may grab or cry before requesting help.

Teacher will place a small communication board near snack and cleanup areas. Family also attends story time at Hazelmere Family Reading Center. Librarian Tavi Morrow reportedly welcomes movement breaks. Family wants pt to participate without pressure to sit through the entire group activity.

6. HEALTH AND DEVELOPMENT REVIEW

Parents report no hospitalization since the prior IFSP. Pediatric visit occurred September 16, 2026. Per the fictional visit summary, growth remained stable and no new activity restrictions were listed. Hearing screening occurred August 20, 2026 at Alderhaven Children’s Pavilion; report documented bilateral pass.

Pt eats varied soft and regular textures. CG reports no coughing, choking, or prolonged meals. SLP observed snack participation without overt distress; this observation does not establish swallowing safety across all foods.

Motor access supports floor play, walking between rooms, and reaching classroom materials. OT Sena Briar previously addressed sensory supports and discharged after family goals were met. Current concern centers on functional communication and participation. Clinical diagnosis recorded for this synthetic episode: ICD-10 F80.2. No speech sound diagnosis was added at review.

7. COMMUNICATION ASSESSMENT AND OBSERVATIONS

SLP used CG interview, bilingual play observation, and MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories: Words and Sentences. Parent-reported English vocabulary raw score: 31. Spanish caregiver inventory contributed additional words; team calculated a descriptive conceptual vocabulary count of 48. Duplicate meanings across languages counted once.

English-only REEL-4 worksheet entries showed receptive standard score 82, expressive standard score 74, and percentiles 12th and 4th, respectively. These entries are retained as test data. They were not used alone to determine bilingual ability or eligibility. Team emphasized functional findings across both languages.

During shared play, pt followed familiar directions in 8/10 opportunities w/ min cues. Pt used intentional requests in 6/10 opportunities w/ mod cues. Sample productions included "ma", "agua", "go", and "all done". Final production occurred after a model. SALT note: [EW] applied to one omitted-word sample.

8. CLINICAL INTERPRETATION AND ACCESS NEEDS

Pt communicates more often when an adult follows his interest, gives one short model, and waits. Longer questions and repeated demands reduced participation during this review. Familiar routines supported understanding better than unfamiliar tabletop tasks.

Speech sample included /m/, /b/, and /d/. SLP heard [w] in an attempted vehicle label. Sample size was insufficient for a full phonological analysis. Team will track functional intelligibility through familiar and unfamiliar listener observations.

Pt benefited from pictures paired w/ natural gestures. Access does not require pointing precisely; touching, looking, handing over a picture, or vocalizing may communicate a choice. CG will acknowledge the message before offering a clearer model. Family will use either language naturally. Team will track whether supports work across people, settings, and daily routines.

9. OUTCOME 1: REQUESTS DURING MEALS

Family outcome: During meals and snack, Nico will communicate a request so CG can respond before frustration increases.

Success criterion: intentional request in 8/10 naturally occurring opportunities across three routine samples, w/ no more than min cues, documented by parent tally and SLP observation. Acceptable forms include gesture, picture, recognizable word, or a combination. Target completion: January 8, 2027.

Strategies: Offer two visible choices. Place a small serving within reach and keep additional food visible. Pause briefly without withholding needed food or drink. Model "more", "más", "water", or "agua" once. Respond to the attempt, then expand the message naturally.

Baseline: requests occurred in 4/10 home opportunities w/ mod cues on October 8, 2026. Mother will tally one breakfast weekly. Father will practice during evening snack. SLP will coach timing and adjust pictures if pt does not understand them. Family may stop practice when pt shows fatigue or distress.

10. OUTCOME 2: HELP AND TRANSITIONS

Family outcome: Pt will communicate a need for help or a wish to finish during dressing, cleanup, and daycare transitions.

Success criterion: use a consistent signal in 4/5 opportunities across home and daycare, w/ min cues, for two consecutive weeks. Target completion: February 5, 2027.

Strategies: Place "help", "ayuda", "finished", and "terminé" pictures where each routine occurs. Adult names the problem, offers one model, and waits. During cleanup, pair the finish picture w/ a predictable closing song. Give warning before changing activities.

Baseline: pt used a help signal in 1/5 observed opportunities w/ max cues. Teacher Ms. Lopez will record brief examples during transitions. CG will offer assistance promptly when distress rises. Team will review whether the task itself needs adjustment; communication practice must not delay comfort, toileting, or access to an adult.

11. OUTCOME 3: SHARED PLAY WITH PEERS

Family outcome: Pt will join a short play exchange w/ another child using an action, gesture, picture, or word.

Success criterion: three reciprocal turns during familiar play in 3/4 observed opportunities, w/ mod cues or less. Target completion: March 4, 2027.

Strategies: Begin w/ parallel play beside Milo Crest or Anya Bellweather. Adult models giving, receiving, and waiting using duplicate toys. Use rolling balls, pouring cups, or simple pretend feeding. Target words may include "turn", "go", "toma", and "mío".

Baseline: one reciprocal turn occurred in 2/4 opportunities. Staff will avoid requiring eye contact or spoken imitation before participation. SLP will coach adults to recognize small bids, including offering a toy or moving closer. Family will practice similar exchanges w/ sibling during evening play, while keeping the sibling role enjoyable.

12. OUTCOME 4: FAMILY CONFIDENCE

Family outcome: CG will feel able to support communication in both languages without turning routines into drills.

Success criterion: each participating CG identifies two useful strategies and demonstrates them during a chosen routine, w/ min cues, across two visits. Family confidence rating will increase from 4/10 to at least 7/10. Target completion: December 10, 2026.

SLP will use observation, reflection, joint planning, and brief coached practice. CG selects the routine before each visit. Aunt receives the same picture set and a plain-language explanation. Grandmother may join a scheduled call if parents request it.

Family will choose a weekly practice focus. SLP will ask what helped, what felt awkward, and what needs changing. A missed practice week will prompt problem-solving around family demands, without adding homework.

13. SERVICES, DATES, AND PAYMENT

Speech-language intervention: individual family coaching, 1x/week, 45 minutes, home as primary natural environment. Provider: Iris Maren-Quill. Service start: October 12, 2026. Authorized end: April 7, 2027. Authorization: SLP-FIC-260041. Billing reference: CPT 92507.

Daycare consultation: included within the planned intervention schedule, approx monthly, by parent agreement. A daycare visit replaces that week’s home visit unless the team formally changes frequency.

Service coordination: 1x/month contact plus additional coordination as needed. Provider: Mara Fenwick. Start: October 8, 2026. End: April 7, 2027. No transportation service requested.

SC will verify funding and send written notice before any family charge. The listed Medicaid identifier is fictional. Missed visits will be rescheduled according to family availability and authorization limits. Team will review frequency if attendance barriers, routine demands, or functional progress change.

14. OTHER AGENCIES AND SUPPORTS

Family receives nutrition support through Hazelmere WIC Family Office, contact 919 555 0153. CG reports current appointments fit the work schedule. No new nutrition referral requested.

Juniper Bend Smart Start Partnership supplied books and a caregiver play guide. Hazelmere County Family Support Services previously helped locate childcare resources; no open protective-services matter was reported.

Sibling’s school contact is teacher Ms. Nella Hart, Juniper Lantern Elementary. School information appears only to describe household routines; the team will not share pt records there without separate consent.

SC offered a parent group through Alderhaven Early Connections Network. Parents declined for now b/c evening attendance is difficult. Referral can be revisited. Team recorded the decision without treating group attendance as necessary for progress.

15. TRANSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Pt approaches the third birthday on June 8, 2027. SC discussed transition options, family choice, and planning steps. Parents want information about preschool services and continued community supports. No preschool placement decision occurred at this review.

With required consent, SC will contact Hazelmere Preschool Access Team. Proposed transition conference: March 11, 2027, 10:00 a.m.. This date remains tentative until participants confirm.

Next progress check: December 10, 2026. Next six-month IFSP review: April 8, 2027. Parents may request an earlier meeting. SLP will bring routine samples and CG ratings; SC will bring service access updates. Team will judge progress by participation across daily routines, including successful communication without spoken words.

16. AGREEMENT AND SIGN-OFF

Parents agreed that these outcomes reflect their current priorities. They confirmed the home address, contact methods, service location, and language preferences during this fictional meeting. SC reviewed confidentiality, consent, complaint options, and how to request records.

Mother Elena de la Cruz approved the plan on October 8, 2026. Father Tomás Vega-Ruiz approved on October 8, 2026. SC Mara Fenwick documented agreement. SLP Iris Maren-Quill completed the review note on October 9, 2026.

Current plan: begin the updated coaching schedule, share agreed pictures w/ daycare, and monitor meal requests first. Family will contact SC if work hours change. All signatures are fictional typed attestations for offline de-identification testing.

North Carolina Infant-Toddler Program
Individualized Family Service Plan Review

FICTIONAL DOCUMENT FOR OFFLINE DE-IDENTIFICATION TESTING

1. DOCUMENT AND REVIEW INFORMATION

1.1 Review identification

This report records a family-centered IFSP review completed on 3 de marzo de 2025. Every person, organization, address, identifier, and event in this document is fictional.

The client is Emilia Lucero Rivas, called Emi by the family. Her birth date is 11/03/2022. Her chronological age at this review is 2;4. The program record number is ITP-5837429, and the Medicaid member number is 947206381Q.

The current plan began on 09-16-2024. This review updates family priorities, functional outcomes, service arrangements, and coordination responsibilities. The next review is scheduled for June 2, 2025.

1.2 Report preparation

Ms. Luciana Varela, a bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist employed by Little Path Bilingual Therapies, prepared this report in English. Spanish was the primary language used during family interviews. The clinician documented the family’s meaning without treating bilingual development as a disability.

2. FAMILY INFORMATION

2.1 Household and contact details

Emilia lives with her mother, Mariela Rivas, her father, Diego Lucero, and her brother, Javier Lucero Rivas. Her sister, Sofía Lucero Rivas, stays in the household on alternate weekends.

The family’s mailing address is 4826 Lantern Fern Lane, Cedar Hollow, North Carolina 27986, in Briar County. The preferred telephone number is (252) 555-0146. Written appointment reminders may be sent to mariela.rivas@familymail.example.

The father works at Fernstead Packing Cooperative. His rotating shifts affect appointment availability. The mother manages most weekday routines and requests advance notice when providers need to change visits.

2.2 Extended family

The maternal grandmother, Rosa Beltrán, provides care twice weekly. The family maintains contact with the grandfather, Tomás Beltrán, whose fictional address is Calle de las Guayabas 27, San Jacinto del Naranjal, Honduras.

The babysitter, Nina Cordero, supports occasional evening care. The family’s dog, Luna, frequently joins floor play.

3. SERVICE COORDINATION AND PARTICIPANTS

3.1 Lead agency

The assigned office is Willow Creek CDSA. Ms. Hannah Mercer serves as the service coordinator. Her telephone number is 252-555-0178, and her email address is hannah.mercer@willowcdsa.example.

The service coordinator confirmed family participation, reviewed procedural information, and recorded agreement with the revised outcomes. The family requested Spanish explanations for forms and English copies for its household folder.

3.2 Review participants

Participants included both parents, the bilingual speech-language pathologist, occupational therapist Priya Desai, physical therapist Owen Brooks, and interpreter Esteban Salcedo.

The interpreter supported discussion of administrative language and checked the family’s understanding. He did not administer standardized testing or independently interpret clinical findings.

The pediatrician, Dr. Camila Serrano, provided a written update dated 02/24/2025. Classroom information came from Ms. Celeste Ibarra and classroom assistant Jonah Bell. Each participant addressed activities within their role.

4. FAMILY CONCERNS AND PRIORITIES

4.1 Family’s own words

The mother stated, “I want Emi to tell us what she needs before she becomes upset. Sometimes she points, and we guess wrong. I want her to ask for help during meals and play.”

The father stated, “When I return from work, I want to understand what happened during her day. I would like her to show me something and use a word, a sign, or a picture.”

The grandmother stated, “I want to know how long to wait. I sometimes give her everything before she has a chance to ask.”

4.2 Ranked priorities

The family selected communication during meals as its first priority. Participation in play and transitions followed. The parents also requested practical ways to explain communication supports to relatives.

The family wants strategies that fit ordinary routines. It prefers brief practice opportunities over separate homework periods. The team agreed that successful participation can include gestures, pictures, signs, Spanish words, English words, or combinations of these forms.

5. STRENGTHS, LANGUAGES, AND INTERESTS

5.1 Child and family strengths

Emilia seeks familiar adults, enjoys shared songs, and brings preferred toys to others. She notices changes in familiar routines and watches an adult’s face before attempting a new action.

The family uses Spanish during most home routines. English occurs during childcare, community activities, and some sibling play. The brother enjoys translating familiar songs, although adults remain responsible for communication support.

The parents identify bubbles, toy animals, kitchen utensils, and books with flaps as strong interests. These materials support shared attention without requiring purchased therapy equipment.

5.2 Communication observations

The child used "más", "agua", and "up" spontaneously during this review. A production of "awa" accompanied a reach toward a cup. The clinician accepted that production as a meaningful approximation of the target word "agua".

The team observed emerging combinations of gestures and vocalizations. Speech clarity varied by context. Familiar listeners understood more when they could see the activity.

6. DAILY ROUTINES AND PARTICIPATION

6.1 Morning and meals

The household usually begins breakfast at 7:15 a.m.. The child sits with a caregiver and chooses between two familiar foods. Communication opportunities include requesting another portion, rejecting an item, and asking for assistance.

Dressing follows breakfast. The mother offers one clothing choice and allows time for a response. The family reports that rushed departures reduce opportunities for participation.

6.2 Childcare, rest, and evening routines

Attendance at Meadow Lantern Child Development Center occurs three mornings weekly. Group play begins at 9:00 a.m., and the family usually collects the child at 12:10 p.m..

Rest begins around 1:30 p.m.. Evening play occurs after dinner, depending on the father’s work schedule. Bath time generally starts at 7:20 p.m..

The brother attends Pineglass Elementary School. His afternoon arrival provides a familiar opportunity for greeting and shared book reading. Providers will build strategies into these routines rather than adding a separate treatment schedule.

7. DEVELOPMENTAL AND HEALTH REVIEW

7.1 Assessment sources

The clinician reviewed caregiver interviews, direct observation, and the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale. Receptive language skills appeared most consistent within the 21–24 months range, with scattered higher skills. Expressive language skills appeared mainly within the 15–18 months range.

These criterion-referenced findings describe observed skills. They do not provide a standard score or establish eligibility independently.

A previous Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition assessment recorded a Language Composite standard score of 78, at the 7th percentile. Interpretation included language exposure, caregiver information, and the limits of the assessment setting.

7.2 Health information

The pediatrician reported no current activity restrictions. A hearing visit at Fernwater Children’s Hospital on 2025/01/28 documented responses at 20 dB HL in sound-field screening.

The family reported no new feeding concerns. The occupational therapist will monitor seating and utensil participation. The physical therapist will monitor safe movement during play.

8. OTHER AGENCIES AND COMMUNITY SUPPORTS

8.1 Active involvement

Briar County DSS assists the family with benefit renewal questions. Caseworker Ms. Alina Foster is the identified contact. No protective services involvement is reported in this fictional case.

Briar County WIC provides nutrition counseling and food benefits. The family requested coordination of appointment reminders because missed transportation has affected attendance.

Briar County Smart Start provides information about lending materials and community play opportunities. Sunfield Early Head Start is reviewing a referral for family support and future enrollment options.

8.2 Coordination responsibilities

The service coordinator will confirm which agencies need updated contact information. Information sharing will follow the family’s documented permissions.

Transportation dispatcher Marcus Hale may arrange rides when requested. The family will receive scheduling information through its preferred contact method.

The team reviewed the fictional resource portal at https://resources.willowcdsa.example/families. Access to this portal is optional and does not determine service eligibility.

9. PROGRESS SINCE THE PREVIOUS PLAN

9.1 Communication progress

During snack observations, Emilia communicated a choice in 6/10 opportunities with min cues. Earlier observations documented 3/10 opportunities with mod cues. Responses included pointing, vocalizing, and selecting a picture.

The child requested help in 2/5 opportunities when an adult paused beside a closed container. She continued to rely on reaching or crying when materials were unavailable or adults moved too quickly.

9.2 Participation progress

The child joined brief turn-taking activities for approximately four minutes when a familiar adult followed her interests. Classroom staff reported more successful participation in songs than in group instructions.

Transitions improved when adults used a familiar object and a short verbal cue. These findings support continued routine-based intervention.

The family reported practicing the strategies on most weekdays. The clinician treated that report as caregiver information, not as independently verified frequency data.

10. OUTCOME ONE: FUNCTIONAL REQUESTS

10.1 Outcome statement and measurement

By 05/30/2025, Emilia will communicate a request, rejection, or request for help during meals and play in 8/10 natural opportunities across three consecutive observations.

Acceptable forms include gestures, signs, pictures, words, and meaningful approximations. Adults will record the situation and response, with no requirement to use English instead of Spanish.

10.2 Strategies

Caregivers will offer two visible choices, pause, and respond to the child’s communication. They will model one useful word without requiring repetition before providing the item.

Target words include "más", "ayuda", "abre", and "help". Models will follow the language already used in the routine.

The clinician will coach caregivers to reduce support from mod cues toward min cues. The family will practice during breakfast, snack, and toy cleanup.

Progress will be reviewed through caregiver examples and direct observation. Providers will revise a strategy when it increases frustration or interrupts participation.

11. OUTCOME TWO: SHARED PLAY AND SOCIAL COMMUNICATION

11.1 Outcome statement

By June 2, 2025, the child will complete four reciprocal play turns with an adult or peer in 4/5 observed opportunities, using objects, gestures, vocalizations, or words.

Peers Nico Aranda and Alma Funes participate in the same classroom play group. Staff will support voluntary interaction and respect each child’s interest in joining.

11.2 Strategies and clinical interpretation

Adults will imitate an action, offer a related action, and pause. Suggested activities include rolling a ball, feeding toy animals, and adding blocks to a shared structure.

The clinician will model targets such as "my turn", "toma", and "go". Speech sounds including /k/ may occur in models, but accurate articulation is not required for success.

A glide production such as [w] will be documented descriptively. Language samples may use SALT conventions, including [EW], when appropriate. Coding will supplement functional observations rather than replace them.

12. OUTCOME THREE: TRANSITIONS AND CAREGIVER CONFIDENCE

12.1 Outcome statement

By 05-30-2025, the family will use two selected transition supports during dressing, childcare departure, and cleanup. The child will participate with manageable distress in 80% of recorded opportunities.

Caregivers will identify which supports helped and whether the routine remained practical. The team will review patterns rather than treating one difficult day as failure.

12.2 Strategies

Adults will show a familiar object or picture before the transition. They will use one short statement, allow processing time, and offer a simple action the child can complete.

The occupational therapist will address clothing and seating demands. The physical therapist will suggest movement options that support safe participation. The speech-language pathologist will help adults pair visual information with understandable language.

The grandmother requested demonstration followed by practice. Coaching will include observation, caregiver reflection, and one agreed adjustment. Written instructions will remain brief and available in the family’s preferred language.

13. SERVICES, FREQUENCY, AND DATES

13.1 Speech-language and coordination services

Speech-language services will occur once weekly for forty-five minutes in the home or childcare routine. The service period is 03/10/2025 through 09/15/2025. The assigned clinician is Ms. Luciana Varela.

The anticipated documentation code is CPT 92507. The recorded diagnosis code is ICD-10 F80.2. These codes describe clinical documentation and do not replace the IFSP outcomes.

Service coordination will continue monthly and as needed. The assigned coordinator is Ms. Hannah Mercer. The coordination authorization is SC-250310-6842.

13.2 Other provider schedules

Occupational therapy will occur twice monthly for forty-five minutes, beginning March 12, 2025. Physical therapy consultation will occur monthly, beginning 2025-03-19.

Interpreter support is scheduled for the next joint meeting on 06/02/2025 at 10:30 a.m.. The family prefers visits after breakfast and before afternoon rest. Providers will confirm appointments rather than assuming a recurring time remains suitable.

14. IMPLEMENTATION, TRANSITION, AND FOLLOW-UP

14.1 Team communication

The service coordinator will maintain the shared service schedule. Providers will document completed visits, missed visits, caregiver priorities, and changes that affect participation.

The family’s old calendar contains the entry el martes 4 de junio. The coordinator identified it as an earlier appointment note. It will not be used to schedule a current service.

The parents requested reminders containing the full date. Numeric dates alone have caused confusion between day-first and month-first formats.

14.2 Transition planning

Transition discussions will begin before the child reaches 3 years. The coordinator will explain available options and obtain the permissions needed for referrals.

The family wants information about classroom language supports, transportation, and opportunities to visit potential settings. The team will document decisions after discussion.

No placement decision was made at this review. Current services will continue under the stated plan while transition questions are addressed.

15. AGREEMENT AND CLINICAL SUMMARY

15.1 Family agreement

The mother, Mariela Rivas, stated, “This plan fits what we need at home. I want everyone to use the same simple steps.”

The father, Diego Lucero, stated, “Please show me the strategies when I am available. Written notes help, but I learn more by practicing.”

The family agreed to the outcomes and requested a Spanish verbal review before signing. The interpreter confirmed that the family could ask questions and describe the plan in its own words.

15.2 Final documentation

The bilingual speech-language pathologist recommends continued coaching within familiar routines. The child’s bilingual exposure will remain part of assessment and intervention planning.

The coordinator will distribute the completed plan according to documented family permissions. The report completion date is 03.04.2025.

Prepared by Ms. Luciana Varela, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist.

Reviewed with Ms. Hannah Mercer, service coordinator.

Client reference: E. L. R..
Record reference: ITP-5837429.

+ Name: Elías Marín Varela
+ CA: 4;2
+ Context: Sesión individual de lenguaje en español, con apoyo bilingüe, en Voces del Laurel Pediatría, Villa Cedruna, Carolina del Norte.

+ Fin: 9:50 a. m.

**Resumen de la sesión**

La patóloga del habla y lenguaje, Natalia Cárdenas Soler, atendió al niño durante cuarenta minutos. Se confirmó la identidad con su mamá, Rocío Varela Montes, y el expediente SLP-604827. La fecha de nacimiento registrada es 7 de agosto de 2022. El número de Medicaid ficticio del expediente es 684209731Q. Se documentó tratamiento individual con CPT 92507 y diagnóstico ICD-10 F80.2.

**S: Información subjetiva**

Su mamá Rocío informó que trabaja de noche como técnica de inventario en Laboratorios Brisa de Ámbar, desde las 10:00 p. m. hasta las 6:00 a. m.. Su papá, Tomás Marín Rueda, prepara el desayuno y practica instrucciones antes de salir. La abuela Inés Montes Rivas recoge al niño de Centro Infantil Nube de Cobre. Su hermana Alma Marín Varela suele responder por él. La familia acordó darle tiempo para contestar.

La maestra Mireya Ponce de Escuela Preescolar Sendero de Luciérnagas reportó que el niño participa más cuando juega con Bruno Cerezo y Nadia Ferral. En casa, llama a su perro Miso para mostrarle juguetes. Hoy llegó descansado y aceptó la transición sin llorar.

**O: Observaciones y actividades**

Elías eligió una caja de animales y mantuvo la atención durante bloques de ocho minutos. Siguió instrucciones de dos pasos en 8/10 oportunidades con claves moderadas. Sin apoyo visual, completó 5/10. Identificó acciones en fotografías con 80 % de precisión. Produjo frases espontáneas de tres a cuatro palabras durante el juego, incluyendo "el perro está dormido" y "yo quiero otro carro".

Para pedir objetos, utilizó "dame la pelota" después de un modelo verbal. En una muestra breve, produjo "dos perro [EW]"; el código se conservó para revisar la marca plural. La terapeuta modeló "dos perros" sin exigir repetición inmediata. El niño repitió el objetivo en 6/8 oportunidades con claves mínimas.

Se trabajó el fonema /k/ en las palabras "casa", "copa" y "queso". Logró 7/10 producciones iniciales con apoyo visual y táctil consentido. Se observó sustitución por [t] en habla espontánea. La producción de [w] apareció en una aproximación durante el juego. No se administraron pruebas estandarizadas hoy. Como referencia, la evaluación del 18 de septiembre de 2026 registró PLS-5 Spanish, puntuación estándar de lenguaje total 83 y percentil 13.

**A: Interpretación clínica**

El niño mostró mejor respuesta cuando recibió modelos breves y opciones concretas. La comprensión disminuyó al retirar las imágenes. Las frases aumentaron durante actividades elegidas por él, pero todavía necesitó apoyo para plurales y secuencias. La participación familiar favoreció la práctica. Los resultados de hoy reflejan desempeño en esta sesión y no constituyen una nueva evaluación. El pediatra Darío Beltrán de Hospital Infantil Prado de Ágata mantiene seguimiento del desarrollo.

**P: Plan**

Continuar semanalmente y revisar avances el 4 de noviembre de 2026. Practicar cinco minutos después de la merienda, a las 4:30 p. m., usando turnos y espera. La coordinadora Eva Luján de CDSA del Condado de Valdelirio recibirá el resumen cuando exista autorización familiar documentada.

El contacto registrado es rocio.varela@example.com, teléfono 919-555-0146. Los materiales están en https://voces-laurel.example.org/familias. La dirección ficticia es 284 Calle del Zafiro, Villa Cedruna, Carolina del Norte, 27688. El conductor Fabián Trejo confirmó la recogida al terminar. La mamá comprendió las recomendaciones y demostró la estrategia de espera.

CONTACTOS Y FUENTES

Madre: Mariela Soto Cárdenas  Teléfono principal: 919-555-0128  Correo: mariela.soto@correo.example
Padre: Diego Valverde Núñez  Teléfono alternativo: +1 984 555 0163

Escuela: Escuela Preescolar Roble de Luna  Maestra: Ms. Lopez  Aula: Ms. Lopez's room
Guardería anterior: Guardería Semillas del Arroyo  Asistente: Sra. Paula Venegas

MOTIVO Y ANTECEDENTES

La familia solicitó esta evaluación por dificultades para expresar ideas completas y para hacerse entender fuera del hogar. La madre indicó que Adrián comprende rutinas conocidas, pero necesita ayuda cuando una instrucción contiene varios pasos. El padre señaló que el niño se frustra cuando otra persona le pide repetir su mensaje. Las dificultades aparecen en ambos idiomas, aunque las oportunidades de usar cada idioma varían.

La remisión pediátrica se emitió el 3 de marzo de 2025. La entrevista inicial ocurrió el 08/19/2025, por teléfono, a las 6:15 p. m.. La familia entregó un cuestionario escolar fechado 22/08/2025. La maestra describió participación adecuada durante canciones y juego libre, con menor participación durante relatos y conversaciones grupales.

Según el cuestionario, Dri suele señalar materiales antes de nombrarlos. Cuando juega con Isabela Ríos, usa frases breves para pedir turnos. Con Tomás Arce, a veces abandona una explicación y entrega el objeto directamente. Estas observaciones se consideraron información funcional; no se usaron como resultados de pruebas estandarizadas.

La familia busca que el niño pueda explicar necesidades, contar experiencias sencillas y participar con mayor independencia. No solicitó eliminar el español ni priorizar exclusivamente el inglés.

HISTORIA DE NACIMIENTO Y SALUD

Lugar de nacimiento: Hospital Materno Aurora del Pinar  Localidad: Puerto Cedral, North Carolina
Fecha registrada: 07/03/2021  Fuente: entrevista familiar y resumen pediátrico
Audición: tamizaje reciente documentado  Fecha: 08-27-2025
Profesional de audiología: Lic. Samuel Cifuentes  Servicio: Centro Auditivo Brisa del Valle

La madre informó un embarazo con atención prenatal regular y sin complicaciones importantes. El nacimiento ocurrió a término. No se reportaron dificultades respiratorias, ingreso a cuidados intensivos ni problemas persistentes de alimentación. El niño regresó al hogar con su familia después de la estancia habitual. Estos antecedentes proceden del relato familiar; no se revisó el expediente obstétrico completo.

Los cuidadores describieron crecimiento estable y controles pediátricos regulares. Informaron episodios ocasionales de otitis, sin colocación de tubos ni cirugía. No reportaron convulsiones, lesiones neurológicas, pérdida de habilidades previamente adquiridas o uso diario de medicamentos. La pediatra recomendó evaluar el lenguaje después de observar frases cortas y dificultades para responder preguntas abiertas.

El resumen de audiología indicó respuestas compatibles con audición funcional para las frecuencias examinadas. Durante esta sesión, Adrián respondió a voces de intensidad conversacional y localizó sonidos ambientales. Estas observaciones no sustituyen una evaluación audiológica completa si aparecen nuevas preocupaciones.

La familia no describió tos frecuente al comer, atragantamiento ni rechazo persistente de texturas. El examen visual de estructuras orales mostró simetría facial y movilidad funcional de labios y lengua para las tareas realizadas. La voz y la resonancia no presentaron diferencias relevantes durante la muestra. No se observaron bloqueos ni tensión asociados con la fluidez.

HISTORIA FAMILIAR Y LINGÜÍSTICA

Domicilio familiar: 718 Camino del Laurel Azul  Municipio: Villa Encino  Estado: North Carolina
Hermana: Renata Valverde Soto  Hermano: Bruno Valverde Soto
Tía: Julia Soto Cárdenas  Cuidadora ocasional: Mónica Leiva
Mascotas: Chispa, perro; Nube, gata

En el hogar se usa principalmente español. La madre conversa, lee cuentos y organiza las rutinas en español. El padre usa español durante comidas y actividades familiares, y algunas expresiones en inglés durante juegos. La hermana Renata alterna ambos idiomas cuando comparte libros. El hermano Bruno participa en juegos de construcción con instrucciones breves.

La abuela Estela mantiene contacto mediante videollamadas desde Villa Naranjal, México. La tía Julia cuida al niño algunas tardes. La cuidadora Mónica usa español y sigue las mismas rutinas de comunicación que los padres. La familia refiere que las mascotas ofrecen oportunidades frecuentes para comentar acciones y pedir ayuda.

Lugar de trabajo materno: Cooperativa Textil Horizonte Claro  Lugar de trabajo paterno: Taller Mecánico Puente Azul
Contacto comunitario: Sr. Óscar Mena  Función: conductor del transporte vecinal

El niño comenzó a asistir a la guardería el martes 4 de junio de 2024. Allí escuchaba español e inglés durante canciones, meriendas y juegos. Ingresó a la escuela actual el 08/18/2025. El horario escolar comienza a las 8:10 a. m. y termina a las 12:40 p. m..

La exposición al inglés ha sido más constante en entornos educativos. El español continúa siendo el idioma de mayor uso familiar. La madre reportó primeras palabras alrededor de 1;6 y combinaciones de palabras cerca de 2;8. No describió regresión. Un tío materno recibió apoyo del habla durante su infancia, según el relato familiar. No se dispone de documentación de ese antecedente.

PROCEDIMIENTOS Y CONDUCTA

Se integraron entrevista, cuestionario, observación de juego, muestra de lenguaje, examen oral y medidas estandarizadas. La evaluación se realizó en español e inglés según los procedimientos de cada instrumento. Los cambios de idioma permitieron explorar conocimientos distribuidos entre ambos idiomas. No se tradujeron reactivos para generar puntuaciones normativas nuevas.

Instrumentos: Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish); Bilingual English–Spanish Assessment (BESA)
Análisis de muestra: Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT)  Contextos: juego, descripción y relato breve

La madre permaneció durante la primera parte de la sesión. Adrián exploró los juguetes y aceptó la interacción con la evaluadora después de un breve periodo de adaptación. Mostró interés por vehículos, animales y una cocina de juguete. La participación mejoró cuando pudo elegir entre dos actividades y anticipar el cambio con una imagen.

Se realizó una pausa a las 9:50 a. m. y se retomaron las tareas a las 10:00 a. m.. El niño permaneció atento durante actividades cortas. Algunas tareas necesitaron redirección, pero no hubo suficiente interferencia conductual para invalidar la interpretación general. Las ayudas adicionales se reservaron para observación clínica y evaluación dinámica.

La interpretación considera la experiencia bilingüe, la familiaridad con los materiales y las diferencias entre tareas estructuradas y comunicación cotidiana. Ninguna puntuación aislada determina las conclusiones. Los resultados descritos pertenecen exclusivamente a este caso ficticio.

RESULTADOS ESTANDARIZADOS

| Instrumento y área | Puntuación estándar | Percentil | Interpretación |
|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish, comprensión auditiva | 79 | 8 | Rendimiento inferior al esperado |
| PLS-5 Spanish, comunicación expresiva | 74 | 4 | Rendimiento inferior al esperado |
| PLS-5 Spanish, lenguaje total | 75 | 5 | Dificultades receptivas y expresivas |
| BESA, semántica, mejor desempeño lingüístico | 82 | 12 | Vulnerabilidad semántica |
| BESA, morfosintaxis, mejor desempeño lingüístico | 73 | 4 | Dificultades morfosintácticas |

Los percentiles representan la posición relativa dentro de la referencia normativa correspondiente. No representan el porcentaje de respuestas correctas. Se consideró el desempeño en ambos idiomas y se contrastó con las observaciones familiares y escolares.

COMPRENSIÓN DEL LENGUAJE

El niño identificó objetos cotidianos y acciones familiares. Siguió instrucciones sencillas cuando el objeto estaba visible. En una tarea clínica, respondió correctamente en 8/10 oportunidades para instrucciones de un paso. Para instrucciones de dos pasos sin apoyo visual, logró 4/10. Estas proporciones describen tareas de observación y no son puntuaciones estandarizadas.

Comprendió relaciones espaciales frecuentes durante el juego. Las dificultades aumentaron cuando debía mantener información verbal, identificar una negación o relacionar dos características simultáneamente. Las preguntas sobre personas y objetos resultaron más fáciles que las preguntas sobre causas y secuencias.

Con imágenes, repetición y claves moderadas (mod cues), mejoró la ejecución. La respuesta a estas ayudas indica capacidad de aprendizaje, aunque todavía requiere apoyo para generalizar. La familia describió un patrón similar al preparar la mochila o recoger materiales. La comprensión fue más sólida en español para vocabulario familiar y variable en inglés para conceptos escolares recientes.

EXPRESIÓN DEL LENGUAJE

La muestra incluyó 52 emisiones analizables. La longitud media fue de 2.9 palabras por emisión. Esta medida se usó de forma descriptiva, sin equipararla directamente con una norma monolingüe. Predominaron peticiones, etiquetas y comentarios sobre acciones presentes.

Entre las producciones espontáneas aparecieron "yo quiere carro", "mamá dame eso" y "perro está aquí". Las palabras objetivo trabajadas durante la exploración fueron "quiero", "porque" y "después". Se observaron omisiones variables de artículos, marcas verbales y elementos necesarios para completar algunas oraciones.

En una tarea de relato, identificó personajes y una acción principal, pero necesitó preguntas específicas para explicar el problema y el resultado. No mantuvo de forma independiente una secuencia completa. Con apoyo visual produjo más información, aunque la organización continuó siendo breve.

El análisis registró [EW] cuando correspondía a errores de palabra según las convenciones utilizadas. La alternancia entre español e inglés se describió por separado. No se clasificó automáticamente como error. Algunas palabras estaban disponibles solamente en uno de los idiomas, lo cual refleja experiencias diferentes y no constituye por sí mismo una dificultad.

HABLA E INTELIGIBILIDAD

La inteligibilidad estimada para una oyente sin familiaridad previa fue de 68% en conversación. La madre comprendió una proporción mayor gracias al contexto y al conocimiento de las rutinas. La claridad disminuyó en frases largas y cuando el niño hablaba con rapidez.

Se observaron sustituciones de velares, incluida la realización de /k/ como [t] en algunas palabras. También aparecieron reducciones de grupos consonánticos y realizaciones variables de vibrantes. Una producción ilustrativa fue "tasa" para el objetivo "casa". En inglés se escuchó [w] por /ɹ/ en palabras aisladas; esta observación requiere interpretación según edad, idioma y contexto.

Durante la exploración dinámica, produjo /k/ en sílabas con modelo y apoyo visual en 6/10 oportunidades. La precisión bajó en palabras espontáneas. No se observaron intentos articulatorios inconsistentes acompañados de esfuerzo marcado. La muestra disponible no permite concluir una dificultad motora específica del habla.

COMUNICACIÓN SOCIAL Y JUEGO

Adrián compartió atención, mostró objetos y buscó ayuda de forma funcional. Usó gestos para complementar mensajes y disfrutó el juego simbólico. Respondió a propuestas sencillas y sostuvo intercambios breves cuando el tema le interesaba.

La dificultad principal durante los intercambios fue ampliar o reparar el mensaje. Después de una solicitud de aclaración, con frecuencia repitió la misma frase. Cuando la evaluadora ofreció opciones, logró agregar información. El contacto visual varió de manera natural según la actividad y no se utilizó como medida aislada de competencia comunicativa.

IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

Los resultados apoyan un perfil de dificultades receptivas y expresivas que afecta la participación cotidiana. La evidencia incluye desempeño reducido en medidas estructuradas, limitaciones observadas en ambos idiomas y preocupaciones coincidentes de la familia y la escuela. La adquisición bilingüe no explica por sí sola este conjunto de hallazgos.

Impresión principal: trastorno del lenguaje receptivo y expresivo  Código: ICD-10 F80.2
Impresión adicional: trastorno de los sonidos del habla  Código: ICD-10 F80.0
Fortalezas: intención comunicativa, juego simbólico, participación familiar y respuesta a apoyos

Las dificultades del habla reducen la claridad del mensaje. Las dificultades del lenguaje limitan su contenido y organización. Ambos componentes requieren atención coordinada. El pronóstico funcional es favorable con intervención constante y oportunidades de práctica en los dos idiomas. La evolución deberá comprobarse mediante datos de participación y desempeño, sin depender únicamente de nuevas puntuaciones normativas.

RECOMENDACIONES Y PLAN

1. Iniciar intervención bilingüe dos veces por semana, con sesiones de treinta minutos. Seleccionar actividades relevantes para el hogar y la escuela. Ajustar la frecuencia según progreso, asistencia y necesidades funcionales.

2. Trabajar instrucciones de dos pasos con objetos y acciones conocidos. Reducir gradualmente las ayudas. Meta inicial: alcanzar 8/10 respuestas correctas con claves mínimas en actividades variadas.

3. Ampliar oraciones para expresar acciones, ubicaciones y causas. Modelar estructuras completas sin exigir repetición constante. Meta inicial: producir mensajes de cuatro palabras o más en 80% de oportunidades con apoyo visual.

4. Enseñar relatos breves mediante imágenes de inicio, problema y resultado. Practicar primero experiencias familiares. Permitir respuestas en cualquiera de los dos idiomas y ampliar el mensaje en el idioma de la actividad.

5. Abordar contrastes de /k/ y /t/ según respuesta al tratamiento. Practicar desde sílabas hasta conversación. Registrar precisión y generalización, con una meta inicial de 80% en palabras con claves mínimas.

6. Mantener el español familiar. Leer cuentos, comentar acciones y ofrecer tiempo para responder. Cuando el niño produzca "yo quiere carro", responder con el modelo "yo quiero el carro" dentro de una interacción natural.

7. Coordinar apoyos con Ms. Lopez. Usar instrucciones breves, imágenes y opciones para responder. Facilitar turnos con Isabela y Tomás sin exigir que otros niños actúen como terapeutas.

8. Revisar avances el 3 de diciembre de 2025. Solicitar nueva consulta auditiva si aparecen cambios de respuesta, molestias o infecciones recurrentes.

CIERRE

La evaluadora explicó los hallazgos en español. La madre expresó comprensión y aceptó el plan propuesto. La comunicación futura se realizará por los contactos registrados. La familia recibirá una copia del informe para compartirla con los profesionales y el personal educativo que autorice.

Firma: Lic. Camila Inés Robledo  Empresa: Servicios Bilingües Sendero Infantil
Fecha de firma: 8 de septiembre de 2025  Hora: 4:20 p. m.  Registro profesional ficticio: NC-SLP-670284
