Leonardo Emilio Valcázar was born at Juniper Bell Regional Hospital in Bellhaven, North Carolina, at 39 weeks gestation. Reported birth weight was 7 pounds, 3 ounces. Delivery was vaginal. The caregiver denied an extended neonatal admission, breathing support, or early feeding concerns.

The family returned home to Alderwick after discharge. The caregiver recalled that the infant responded to voices, smiled during face-to-face play, and enjoyed songs in Spanish. Early motor milestones were described as sitting at approximately 7 months and walking at approximately 14 months. First meaningful words appeared at approximately 18 months. Consistent combinations emerged around 30 months.

These milestone ages are caregiver estimates. No original birth record was available for review. The caregiver emphasized that early communication involved many gestures: “Nos llevaba de la mano, pero sí nos miraba para ver si entendíamos.” The child reportedly used pointing, giving, and showing before he used consistent spoken requests. The family did not describe a loss of previously established words or social skills.

Historia médica / Medical history

Dr. Gabriel Tovar provides pediatric care at Cedar Lantern Children's Medical Center. The supplied referral dated September 24, 2026 listed concerns about speech clarity and language development. The caregiver reported seasonal congestion and several childhood ear infections. No current medication, surgery, seizure history, or food allergy was reported. These statements reflect the caregiver interview, not independent medical verification.

An audiology report from Juniper Bell Regional Hospital, dated August 20, 2026, documented responses within the expected range for the tested frequencies. That fictional report was reviewed for this assessment. Today's visit did not include a complete audiologic evaluation. The family reported no new hearing concern since that appointment.

Occupational therapist Tessa Arce sees the child through Willow Lantern Pediatric Communication for participation in dressing and fine motor routines. Physical therapist Owen Salcedo previously addressed balance during playground activities. The caregiver stated that physical therapy ended after functional goals improved. Neither provider attended today's session. Their names appear for care coordination; their findings were not substituted for direct speech-language assessment.

Sleep was described as generally consistent. Breakfast usually occurs around 7:15 a.m., and the family reported that the child ate before this appointment. No discomfort or illness interrupted testing.

Familia, cuidadores e idiomas / Family and language history

Leo lives with his mamá, Inés Valcázar, his papá, Daniel Roldán, and his sister, Alma Roldán. The family also spends time with grandmother doña Lupe, aunt Beatriz Mena, and cousins Nicolás Mena and Eva Mena. The cousins are relatives and are identified here as family members, although both are children.

Spanish is the main language during meals, family visits, and bedtime stories. English appears in school routines, some television programs, and play with the sister. Mamá estimated language exposure as approximately 65% Spanish and 35% English across a typical week. These estimates describe opportunity, not measured proficiency. The family reported frequent switching between languages without concern: “En casa decimos ‘put your shoes aquí,’ porque así sale natural.”

The babysitter, Miss Ana, uses Spanish during afternoon care. She reportedly understands familiar messages and encourages the child to explain instead of answering for him. The family's dog, Chispa, often joins floor play. The child reportedly gives the dog short commands and describes where the dog hides toys.

Mamá works for Cedarloom Textile Services, and papá works for Finchbrook Equipment Repair. Their schedules affect who attends appointments. The household contact address is 7264 Sparrow Lantern Lane, Alderwick, North Carolina 27593. The caregiver contact number is (984) 555-0172. The family requested written information in Spanish and brief English summaries for school.

Participación escolar / Classroom participation

At school, classmates Maya Solís, Julián Vega, and Benji Calder are frequent play partners. According to the classroom questionnaire, Leo approaches these classmates and shares materials. He may repeat a peer's phrase to enter play, then use gestures when the activity becomes less predictable. Staff reported that peers sometimes finish his message.

La maestra Carmen wrote that the child follows the visual arrival routine and enjoys music. Difficulty increases during group explanations, especially when instructions include several actions. Ms. Nadia Paredes reported that a quiet check-in after the group direction often helps. Classroom observations were reported by staff; the clinician did not observe the school directly.

The family also described greetings with a neighbor, Mr. Tom, near the home. These exchanges are short and familiar. The child reportedly says hello readily but needs help explaining where he is going. Successful greetings therefore do not establish that longer conversation is equally easy.

School begins at 8:20 a.m., and pickup occurs at 2:35 p.m.. The family asked that appointments avoid the transition immediately before pickup. Staff requested practical strategies for centers, snack, and playground communication rather than additional worksheets.

Procedimiento y validez / Assessment procedures

The interview began at 9:05 a.m.. Direct assessment began at 9:22 a.m.. A movement break occurred from 9:57 a.m. to 10:04 a.m.. Results and recommendations were discussed from 10:25 a.m. until the session ended at 10:42 a.m..

Marisol Varela conducted assessment in Spanish and English. Interpreter Elena Quirós supported portions of the caregiver interview and checked the clarity of written explanations. The interpreter did not translate standardized test items during administration. When the clinician changed wording or provided teaching, those responses were recorded as descriptive information.

Activities included caregiver interview, review of supplied records, standardized language testing, an English articulation task, oral mechanism observation, pretend play, picture description, and dynamic teaching. The child wore no hearing devices or glasses. He tolerated the room, accepted breaks, and returned to the table with a visual reminder.

Performance varied with familiarity and linguistic demand. Fatigue affected the final picture-description items. Scores describe performance under these conditions. They do not represent a complete measure of communication across every setting or either language. No score alone determined the clinical impression.

Resultados / Test results

| Measure | Domain or condition | Score | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish) | Auditory Comprehension | Standard score 84; percentile 14 | Relative receptive strength; difficulty with complex directions |
| PLS-5 Spanish | Expressive Communication | Standard score 77; percentile 6 | Reduced independent sentence formulation |
| PLS-5 Spanish | Total Language | Standard score 79; percentile 8 | Below the expected range within this fictional profile |
| Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) | English picture naming | Standard score not reported | Descriptive analysis because language experience limits interpretation |
| Dynamic direction task | Familiar actions with visual support | 8/10 correct | Improved access with contextual support |
| Dynamic direction task | Unfamiliar directions without visual support | 4/10 correct | Increased difficulty as task demand rose |
| Functional speech sample | Familiar listener estimate | 72% intelligible | Context supported understanding |
| Functional speech sample | Unfamiliar listener estimate | 48% intelligible | Frequent clarification required |
| Narrative teaching probe | Events stated independently before teaching | 1/5 elements | Limited initial organization |
| Narrative teaching probe | Events stated after teaching | 4/5 elements with mod cues | Positive response to explicit support |

The PLS-5 Spanish scores reflect the administered bilingual scoring procedures in this fictional case. Qualitative findings remain central to interpretation. The English articulation task supplied examples of speech patterns; it did not establish an English-only diagnostic cutoff. Listener estimates came from this session and should not be treated as fixed percentages for all situations.

Lenguaje receptivo / Receptive language

Leo identified familiar objects, understood routine action words, and responded to simple questions during play. He followed a direction to place the toy animal under the chair when the objects were visible. He also matched several actions across Spanish and English without needing an exact translation.

Difficulty appeared when instructions required remembering an order, comparing attributes, or selecting an object from unfamiliar vocabulary. The child sometimes completed the last action mentioned and omitted the earlier action. He benefited from a gesture and a pause between steps. En español, familiar wording improved access, pero the longer direction still required support.

For example, the clinician first presented a direction involving a cup, spoon, and plate. The child moved the plate only. After the clinician showed the sequence and repeated it slowly, he completed the remaining actions. This pattern suggests that processing demand affected success. It does not show that the child lacked all the individual words.

During picture questions, answers were more accurate for visible actions than for why or prediction questions. The clinician accepted responses in either language. Code-switching did not count as an error. When the child supplied a correct concept in English after a Spanish prompt, the response contributed to the descriptive account of conceptual knowledge.

Lenguaje expresivo / Expressive language

Spontaneous communication included requests, comments, protests, and short explanations. Leo used words from both languages and sometimes combined them within a sentence. Examples included “quiero el blue carro” and “he está sleeping”. These productions show flexible use of available vocabulary. The language switch itself was not treated as evidence of impairment.

The main concern was limited sentence organization when the message required more information. The child often omitted a person, action, or location needed by the listener. He relied on “ese”, “allá”, and “the thing” when a specific word did not come readily. Familiar adults supplied the missing context; an unfamiliar listener could not always do so.

Spanish samples included inconsistent article and verb forms. English samples included omitted auxiliaries and limited tense marking. Some forms could reflect developing bilingual experience. The broader concern was that reduced elaboration and weak message repair occurred in both languages, including familiar Spanish routines.

When the clinician modeled a complete sentence, the child usually attempted a longer response. He needed min cues for a practiced request and mod cues for an unfamiliar explanation. A sentence frame helped initially, but he did not consistently use the same structure with a new picture. The assessment therefore distinguished immediate imitation from independent generalization.

Muestra de lenguaje / SALT-style sample

A play sample used a toy kitchen, animals, vehicles, and a brief picture sequence. The clinician collected connected speech in both languages. Sample analysis was descriptive because the setting and bilingual distribution did not support a direct comparison with a matched reference sample.

Selected productions included “doggie se cayó”, “yo poner aquí”, “no, ese mío”, and “then baby cry”. The first production was understandable with the toy event visible. The final production required a follow-up question because the listener did not know which character the child meant.

The sample used [EW] for an extraneous word and [EU] for an utterance-level error annotation where appropriate. These codes describe transcription decisions; they are not separate diagnoses. An unintelligible segment was recorded with X. Repeated attempts were retained when they showed how the child repaired a message.

The child produced longer messages after the clinician used expansion. Following “baby cry”, the clinician modeled “the baby is crying because the cup fell”. The child responded, “baby crying, cup cayó”. This response added relevant information while retaining mixed language.

During the narrative probe, the clinician taught a simple sequence: who, what happened, and how it ended. Performance improved from 1/5 elements to 4/5 elements with mod cues. The improvement supports teaching potential. Continued cueing shows that the skill was not yet independent.

Habla y sonidos / Speech sound findings

Speech clarity varied with word length, familiarity, and sentence complexity. The child produced several early consonants consistently in short words. Accuracy decreased during longer spontaneous messages. The examiner heard substitutions, cluster reduction, and inconsistent syllable omission in both language samples.

Examples included “tat” for the target “cat” and “pato” for the intended target “plato”. These examples represent elicited productions in this fictional session. Analysis considered the sound structure of each language. A pattern expected from cross-language influence was not automatically counted as a disorder.

The child sometimes replaced /k/ with /t/ in English targets. In Spanish, consonant combinations containing /l/ were difficult during connected speech. The clinician also heard [w] in some attempts at English /ɹ/. That observation was documented without making it an immediate treatment priority.

Stimulability improved with a visual mouth model and a slowed production. The child achieved 6/10 correct attempts at /k/ in supported syllables with mod cues. Accuracy fell when cues were removed. The clinician did not observe consistent groping, marked vowel distortion, or a clear pattern sufficient to identify a motor speech disorder during this visit.

Social communication, juego y regulación

Leo showed shared enjoyment, offered toys, checked the adult's response, and invited participation. He used gaze, pointing, and words together. He accepted an adult's play idea and later introduced his own. These behaviors supported reciprocal interaction during the assessment.

Communication became less effective when the listener misunderstood. The child first repeated the same phrase, sometimes louder. After coaching, he pointed to the relevant object or added a word. He benefited from the prompt “show me and tell me one more thing”. Adults should recognize these attempts and give enough time for repair.

Attention varied with task demand. Movement and a clear finish point helped the child return to testing. The caregiver reported similar benefit at home. The examiner did not interpret movement during difficult language tasks as evidence of a separate attention diagnosis.

Oral mechanism, voice, and feeding observations were limited to screening. Facial symmetry and visible oral structures appeared adequate for the sampled tasks. Voice sounded comfortable. No persistent dysfluency was observed. The caregiver denied current chewing or swallowing concerns. A snack was not assessed, so this report does not establish feeding safety.

Impresiones clínicas / Clinical impressions

The fictional profile supports a mixed receptive-expressive language concern with a stronger expressive component and an accompanying speech sound disorder. Difficulties affected message completeness, narrative organization, and intelligibility. They appeared across Spanish and English tasks and were also described in familiar home routines.

Clinical coding for this synthetic record is F80.2 for mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and F80.0 for phonological disorder. The evaluation service code is CPT 92523. These codes are included as protected clinical content for the testing scenario.

Bilingual development contributes to variation in vocabulary and grammatical forms. It does not fully account for the functional difficulties observed here. Interpretation rests on converging information, including caregiver concern, classroom reports, performance across languages, and response to teaching. The child demonstrated useful learning strengths. Support should build on those strengths while preserving access to both languages.

Recomendaciones / Recommendations

1. Begin bilingual speech-language therapy with Marisol Varela at Willow Lantern Pediatric Communication. The proposed schedule is 2 sessions per week, each lasting 30 minutes, for an initial 12-week treatment block. Adjust the schedule according to participation and progress.

2. Target functional messages that identify the person, action, and important detail. Start with familiar play and daily events. Accept Spanish, English, and mixed-language responses. Model a slightly longer sentence without requiring the child to repeat every adult model.

3. Teach message repair directly. Practice adding a word, showing the object, or changing the explanation after a listener signals confusion. Use min cues when possible. Record when the child still requires mod cues.

4. Select speech targets that improve everyday clarity in the child's languages. Begin with stimulable sounds and useful words. Include /k/ practice when it supports functional vocabulary. Reassess sound priorities as connected speech improves.

5. Support classroom directions with a visual sequence and a brief individual check. La maestra Carmen and Ms. Nadia Paredes can ask the child to show the next action. Avoid repeated questioning when a model would clarify the task.

6. Coach family members during short routines. Mamá Inés Valcázar, papá Daniel Roldán, and Miss Ana can expand one message during play or snack. Doña Lupe can continue Spanish stories and songs. Consistent practice matters more than changing the family's language.

7. Coordinate language demands with occupational therapist Tessa Arce. Use the same visual steps during dressing and cleanup. Contact physical therapist Owen Salcedo only if movement concerns again affect participation. Obtain caregiver authorization before sharing the report.

8. Review progress using spontaneous messages, listener understanding, and classroom participation. A useful initial target is a complete functional message in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Compare performance across familiar and unfamiliar activities.

Seguimiento / Follow-up

The caregiver selected a proposed treatment time of 3:45 p.m.. The first appointment is tentatively listed for October 16, 2026. Scheduling staff must confirm availability. A progress review is planned for January 8, 2027. These entries are proposed dates within the fictional record.

During feedback, Leo returned to play while mamá reviewed the recommendations. The caregiver stated, “Sí, queremos que tenga palabras para explicar, en los dos idiomas.” The clinician provided a Spanish summary and an English school handout. No school contact occurred during this visit.

Report completed on October 10, 2026 by Marisol Varela, MS, CCC-SLP. Questions may be directed to (919) 555-0146 or marisol.varela@willowlantern.example. All people, places, organizations, contact details, identifiers, events, and clinical findings in this document are fictional.

text:
EVALUACIÓN DEL HABLA Y LENGUAJE / SPEECH-LANGUAGE ASSESSMENT

- Document status: Entirely fictional clinical report created for offline de-identification testing. All people, organizations, contact details, identifiers, locations, and clinical findings are invented. The assessment narrative and score values describe a synthetic case. Standardized instrument names identify clinical tools and are retained as clinical content.
- Client: Adrián Emiliano Varela Soto. Preferred name: Adrián. Family nickname: Adri. Date of birth: 03/03/2021. Chronological age at evaluation: 4;2. Pronouns: he/him. Languages heard and used: Spanish and English. State of residence: North Carolina.
- Evaluation date: 05/06/2025. Session: 9:15 a.m.–11:05 a.m.. Report completed: May 12, 2025. Referral received: 3 de marzo de 2025. Planned review: 08-12-2025. Service setting: outpatient pediatric clinic with parent participation.
- Evaluating bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist: Elena Marisol Cárdenas, MS, CCC-SLP. Employer: Puente Claro Pediatric Communication Services. Clinic address: 4287 Lantern Finch Drive, Suite 206, Bellmere, NC 27684. Telephone: (919) 555-0146. Secure contact: ecardenas@puenteclaro.example. Website: https://puenteclaro.example.

DATOS ADMINISTRATIVOS / ADMINISTRATIVE INFORMATION

- Medical record number: PCP-25-04682. Medicaid ID: 748205193Q. Secondary insurance: Cedar Lantern Family Health Plan. Insurance member ID: CLF-008461297. Evaluation authorization number: AUTH-SLP-250506-731. Historical NC ITP child ID: ITP-NC-00492861. These identifiers belong only to this fictional record.
- Parent contacts: mother Lucía Varela Soto and father Benjamín Varela Ruiz. Home address: 1632 Willow Kite Lane, Apartment 4B, Bellmere, NC 27684. Mother’s telephone: 984-555-0173. Father’s telephone: 919.555.0128. Family email: familia.varela@correo.example. Preferred contact language: Spanish; written summaries may include English school terms.
- Educational placement: Little Lantern Bilingual Learning House. Receiving preschool program: Cedarwing Early Learning School. County service area: Marigold County. Historical early intervention office: Marigold Children’s Developmental Services Agency. Family resource contact: Bellmere Family Start Collaborative. Records reviewed included parent questionnaires, classroom notes, and a previous transition summary.
- Billing references: speech-language evaluation CPT 92523; anticipated individual treatment CPT 92507. Referral diagnosis: ICD-10 F80.9. Evaluation impressions support consideration of ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0. These codes accompany clinical findings and do not establish educational eligibility or insurance coverage.

MOTIVO DE REFERENCIA / REASON FOR REFERRAL

- The family requested evaluation because Adrián speaks readily at home but becomes difficult to understand when explaining events. His mother reported, “Tiene muchas ideas, pero se le quedan atoradas.” She wants him to request help, tell what happened during play, and communicate comfortably with relatives who speak Spanish.
- His father described concern about both understanding directions and producing clear speech. “Si digo una cosa, la hace; si digo dos, me mira y espera.” The family does not want Spanish removed from daily routines. Their goal is stronger communication across both languages, con palabras que sirvan en la vida diaria.
- Classroom staff reported that Adri joins familiar songs, labels preferred toys, and follows routines supported by pictures. Difficulties appear during unfamiliar instructions, peer negotiation, and group explanations. The referral asks whether observed differences reflect bilingual development, a communication disorder, or a combination requiring language-access supports and intervention.

FUENTES Y PROCEDIMIENTOS / SOURCES AND PROCEDURES

- Information came from interviews with both parents, direct observation, structured play, speech sampling, oral mechanism screening, and selected standardized tasks. The clinician reviewed a pediatric note dated 04/18/2025, a classroom questionnaire dated 2025-04-29, and the historical IFSP dated 02/20/2024. Parent report and observed performance are distinguished throughout.
- Formal instruments included Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish) and Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3). Supplemental tasks used familiar objects, picture sequences, and parent-selected vocabulary. English articulation findings were interpreted alongside Spanish speech patterns. No English-only task was used alone to determine the overall bilingual language impression.
- The clinician completed a brief teach-and-retest activity and collected a bilingual play sample. Sample annotations followed selected Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) conventions. This was a descriptive sample, not a normative database comparison. The interpreter Rosa Inés Beltrán supported administrative discussion only; the evaluating clinician conducted all Spanish-language assessment tasks directly.

ANTECEDENTES / DEVELOPMENTAL BACKGROUND

- According to his mother, Adrián sat independently at approximately 7 months, walked at 14 months, and used recognizable first words near 18 months. Two-word combinations became consistent around 2;8. The family recalls gradual progress without a clear loss of previously established words, social interest, or play skills.
- His parents describe him as observant, affectionate, and persistent with construction toys. He enjoys sorting vehicles, pretending to cook, and helping match socks. When adults ask rapid questions, he may repeat the last word or move away. With extra wait time, he often returns and attempts a longer message.
- Previous early intervention consisted of parent coaching and developmental support. Service coordinator Nora Estela Quintero documented transition planning before the third birthday. The family attended a preschool information meeting on el martes 4 de junio de 2024. No prior comprehensive bilingual speech-language evaluation was available for comparison.

HISTORIA DEL NACIMIENTO / BIRTH HISTORY

- Mother reported pregnancy monitoring for mild anemia, treated with a prescribed supplement. Prenatal care occurred at Bellmere Valley Women’s Hospital. Delivery was at 39 weeks, 2 days by uncomplicated vaginal birth. Reported birth weight was 7 pounds, 3 ounces. These details came from parent recall; original delivery records were unavailable.
- Adrián reportedly stayed with his mother after delivery and went home after routine observation. Parents denied a neonatal intensive care admission, feeding tube, prolonged oxygen support, or known birth injury. Mother recalled early latch difficulty that improved with feeding support. The family did not report persistent coughing or color change during infant feeds.
- Newborn hearing screening reportedly passed in both ears. The parents could not provide the original screening form. No clinician inferred current hearing status from that historical report. The distinction matters because speech and language access can change after infancy, especially when families report later ear symptoms or inconsistent responses.

HISTORIA MÉDICA / MEDICAL HISTORY

- Primary care physician Samuel Iván Duarte follows routine development and general health. Parents reported two treated ear infections during the previous winter and occasional seasonal congestion. They denied seizures, major head injury, known genetic diagnosis, and current daily prescription medication. The synthetic medical history contains no verified outside laboratory or imaging results.
- An audiology appointment at Marigold River Children’s Hospital was scheduled for 05/22/2025 at 10:40 a.m.. Audiologist Priya Celeste Raman was listed on the referral. During this evaluation, responses to conversational speech were adequate in the quiet room, but this observation does not replace ear-specific hearing assessment.
- Parents described sleep as generally settled, with occasional waking after congestion. Food preferences include soft fruit, beans, rice, and crunchy snacks. They denied recurring choking or unexplained weight loss. Feeding was not a referral concern. The clinician observed comfortable water drinking without overt difficulty and did not complete a swallowing evaluation.

FAMILIA Y CUIDADORES / FAMILY AND CAREGIVERS

- Adrián lives with both parents and his sister Marina Varela Soto, age 7 years. His brother Nicolás Varela Soto, age 10 months, also lives in the home. Parents described predictable evening routines, shared meals, and frequent family storytelling. His sister sometimes answers for him when adults wait too briefly.
- Maternal grandmother doña Lupe provides care on two afternoons each week. An aunt, Teresa Alondra Soto, visits regularly. Babysitter Inés Paloma Ríos uses Spanish during meals and neighborhood walks. Grandmother reported, “Conmigo habla más despacito; si le doy tiempo, me cuenta.” Caregiver interviews suggested stronger participation when listeners accept gestures and partial verbal messages.
- Extended family members live in San Jacintito de las Nubes, Mexico. The mailing address used for a maternal uncle is Calle del Guayabo 27, Barrio Las Campanas, San Jacintito de las Nubes, 68473. Uncle Óscar Mateo Soto joins video calls. The family’s dog, Canela, often becomes a topic during those conversations.

HISTORIA DE IDIOMAS / LANGUAGE EXPOSURE

- Spanish has been present from birth and remains the main language for family stories, caregiving, and discipline. English exposure increased after daycare entry at 2;6. Parents estimated current waking exposure at approximately 65% Spanish and 35% English. These estimates describe opportunities to hear language, not measured proficiency or fixed language dominance.
- Mother uses mostly Spanish. Father uses Spanish with occasional English work terms from Blue Finch Packing Cooperative, his workplace. The sister brings English songs and classroom phrases home. A typical family exchange may begin in Spanish and finish in English. Code-switching is accepted and does not itself indicate confusion or impairment.
- During the session, Adri selected Spanish for family topics and mixed languages during vehicle play. He said "mira, the truck cayó", then pointed to the fallen toy. Both languages contributed meaning. The clinician credited conceptual knowledge across languages when allowed by the assessment procedure and documented other bilingual responses descriptively.

ESCUELA Y PARTICIPACIÓN / CLASSROOM PARTICIPATION

- Lead teacher Miss Ana completed the questionnaire. Spanish enrichment teacher la maestra Carmen described stronger responses during small-group activities. Classroom assistant Joel Esteban Paredes reported that picture choices reduce frustration. Staff agreed that Adrián seeks participation, though listeners sometimes misunderstand his requests during noisy transitions.
- Classmates Luna Isabel Rojas and Felipe Andrés Mora frequently join his block play. Another group member, Sofía Elena Paz, often models short pretend-play phrases. Teachers reported successful sharing when adults provide a visual turn marker. Unclear speech sometimes causes peers to hand him the wrong object, followed by pointing or repeated requests.
- School transportation driver Mr. Tom reportedly understands familiar greetings but asks classroom staff to clarify longer messages. The family identified this as a practical concern during arrival. Teacher observations suggest that predictable routines support performance, while unfamiliar listeners and competing noise increase communication demands. The report recommends examining both language skills and environmental supports.

OBSERVACIONES / BEHAVIORAL OBSERVATIONS

- Adrián entered holding a small toy bus and initially stayed close to his mother. After a short warm-up, he explored the room and invited the clinician into play. Eye gaze, showing objects, shared enjoyment, and spontaneous social bids were observed. He used pointing and facial expressions effectively when verbal messages were incomplete.
- Attention was best during hands-on tasks lasting approximately 5–7 minutes. He needed movement breaks between picture-based activities. When a task became difficult, he sometimes said "no sé", pushed a card away, or looked toward his mother. Gentle modeling and a clear endpoint helped him resume without pressure to repeat every response.
- Performance varied with familiarity, sentence length, and available context. The clinician used a visual schedule, offered language choices, and accepted mixed-language messages during informal tasks. No behavioral diagnosis was made. The observed hesitation appeared linked to communication demands within this session, though a single visit cannot establish behavior across every setting.

EXAMEN ORAL Y VOZ / ORAL MECHANISM AND VOICE

- Facial appearance and oral structures were adequate for the observed speech tasks. Lip closure, tongue movement, and jaw opening were functionally demonstrated during imitation and play. The clinician did not identify an obvious structural barrier to speech production. This brief screening did not include instrumentation, a dental examination, or a detailed cranial nerve assessment.
- Voice was comfortable in pitch and loudness for conversational interaction. Resonance sounded generally balanced during the available sample. Parents did not report persistent hoarseness. No consistent audible struggle accompanied speech. The clinician observed occasional repetitions during formulation, but the sample did not establish a fluency disorder or support a separate fluency diagnosis.
- Speech coordination improved when the clinician slowed the model and reduced utterance length. He could imitate /p/, /m/, and /t/ accurately in simple syllables. Attempts involving /k/ and /g/ were less consistent. These findings describe task performance and should be considered with connected speech and stimulability observations.

RESULTADOS / SCORE TABLE

- The following scores are synthetic values for this fictional report. Standard scores, confidence intervals, and percentiles are retained as clinical tokens. Language scores reflect administration of the bilingual instrument within its procedures. The English articulation score has limited standalone interpretive value because the child’s language experience and cross-language speech patterns require additional analysis.

  | INSTRUMENT / SCALE | STANDARD SCORE | PERCENTILE | CONFIDENCE INTERVAL | INTERPRETIVE NOTE |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension | 77 | 6th | 72–84 | Below expected performance |
  | PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication | 74 | 4th | 69–82 | Below expected performance |
  | PLS-5 Spanish Total Language | 74 | 4th | 70–81 | Needs contextual interpretation |
  | GFTA-3 Sounds-in-Words | 70 | 2nd | 65–78 | English task; descriptive caution |

- Standardized results support concerns raised by the family, but scores do not describe every communication strength. The clinician considered language exposure, functional participation, informal tasks, and response to teaching. No age-equivalent score is reported. A single summary number would conceal the difference between familiar routine vocabulary and the language needed for unfamiliar explanations.

COMPRENSIÓN / RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE

- Adrián identified familiar objects and actions in either language. He followed single-step directions with contextual support in 8/10 opportunities. Directions involving two distinct actions were correct in 4/10 opportunities without gesture support. Performance improved to 7/10 when the clinician added pictures and repeated the direction once at a slower pace.
- Understanding of location words was uneven. He demonstrated "in", "on", and "adentro", but responses to "behind", "debajo", and "between"] were inconsistent. Some errors appeared in both languages after familiar vocabulary was established. This pattern suggests a need to teach concepts explicitly rather than assume translation alone will resolve difficulty.
- He answered concrete object questions more readily than questions about reasons or sequence. For a picture story, he identified the main action but needed choices to explain why a character was upset. Como apoyo, the clinician paired spoken questions with pointing and brief models. Reduced memory demands improved responses without eliminating all difficulty.

EXPRESIÓN / EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE

- Spontaneous messages were usually short combinations of words, gestures, and occasional sound effects. Adri said "mamá, dame carro rojo", "he fall down", and "yo no tengo ese". He communicated requests more easily than explanations. Longer messages often omitted information that an unfamiliar listener needed to understand the event.
- Descriptive probes showed frequent verb and grammatical omissions beyond isolated cross-language transfer examples. He named actions correctly in 9/12 opportunities but produced complete agent-action-object descriptions in 4/12. With a visual sentence strip and mod cues, performance increased to 8/12. Responses remained variable when the visual support was removed.
- Parent-supported storytelling yielded more detail than direct questioning. Mother introduced a familiar cooking routine, and he added who stirred, what spilled, and where the spoon went. His longest messages occurred when the listener waited. This suggests useful learning conditions, aunque todavía necesita ayuda to organize a message and include the listener’s missing information.

MUESTRA DE LENGUAJE / LANGUAGE SAMPLE

- The clinician analyzed 50 complete, intelligible utterances from bilingual play. Mean length of utterance was 3.1 morphemes using the stated descriptive counting approach. Because mixed-language morphology and sample context affect interpretation, this value was not compared directly with an English-only normative reference. The sample included requests, comments, protests, and a few questions.
- Selected annotations included [EW] for extraneous words and [EU] for utterance-level errors under the sample’s coding conventions. These codes describe transcription decisions, not diagnostic labels. The child production "the niño go ahí" conveyed an understandable idea despite mixed language. Code-switching itself was not assigned an error code.
- Communication breakdowns increased when pronouns lacked clear referents or event descriptions omitted the actor. After clarification, Adrián sometimes repeated the same phrase more loudly instead of adding detail. With a model, he could repair by naming the object or person involved. Repair strategies therefore represent a practical treatment target across home and classroom routines.

HABLA Y ESTIMULABILIDAD / SPEECH AND STIMULABILITY

- Connected speech showed recurring fronting of velar targets and reduction of some consonant clusters. Examples included "tasa" for "casa", "tat" for "cat", and "pato" for "plato". The clinician distinguished shared patterns from language-specific differences. English final consonant performance was examined with attention to Spanish influence and individual word familiarity.
- Familiar-listener intelligibility was estimated at 75% during contextual play. The clinician’s estimate for unfamiliar-listener understanding was approximately 55% when context was reduced. These are observational estimates, not standardized scores. Mother understood more when she knew the topic. Longer messages and faster rate increased the number of requests for repetition.
- With placement cues and a visual model, Adrián produced /k/ in syllables in 6/10 trials and /g/ in 5/10 trials. Without cues, accuracy decreased. Occasional [w] substitutions were noted in English liquid targets. These findings support staged practice beginning with stimulable forms and progressing toward meaningful words.

APRENDIZAJE / DYNAMIC ASSESSMENT

- During a brief teaching task, the clinician modeled how to describe a picture using who, action, and object. Initial independent completeness was 3/8. After guided practice with mod cues, completeness reached 6/8. A short delayed probe yielded 4/8 without the sentence strip, showing partial learning with continued support needs.
- Adrián benefited from repeated meaningful models, visual organization, and time to respond. He did not benefit from rapid correction after every attempt. The clinician used recasts such as "el perro está corriendo" after shorter messages, then continued play. Parents practiced the same approach successfully during the session.
- Modifiability was present, but carryover was inconsistent. This finding supports a learning plan with repeated opportunities across settings. It does not erase the concerns shown in both languages. The clinician would expect follow-up data to clarify which supports can be faded and which remain necessary for independent classroom participation.

IMPRESIONES / CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

- The combined findings are consistent with a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder in this synthetic case. Concerns appear across languages and include following unfamiliar directions, organizing messages, and expressing grammatical relationships. Bilingual exposure does not adequately explain the full pattern. The impression relies on converging functional evidence as well as standardized results.
- Findings also support a speech sound disorder characterized by reduced intelligibility and recurring speech patterns affecting shared sounds. Some English productions may reflect Spanish influence and should receive separate descriptive treatment. Targets should improve communication in both languages. The clinician should avoid treating an expected accent difference as a disorder.
- Strengths include social engagement, interest in shared play, useful gestures, family involvement, and response to structured teaching. Hearing status remains pending formal assessment. This report does not diagnose autism, attention disorders, intellectual disability, or a swallowing disorder. Educational eligibility requires the receiving team’s evaluation and consideration of educational impact.

RECOMENDACIONES / PLAN DE APOYO

- Begin bilingual speech-language intervention with functional goals. A proposed schedule is 1 session weekly for 12 weeks, then review progress. Initial language goals should address supported directions, clear event descriptions, and communication repair. Initial speech goals should address stimulable shared targets in meaningful vocabulary, with practice connected to family and classroom activities.
- Use short models during daily routines: say one useful phrase, pause, and allow a response. Accept Spanish, English, gestures, and mixed messages. Add a small amount of information to the child’s message without requiring constant repetition. Family language choices should preserve comfortable conversation with relatives and access to both languages.
- Classroom supports should include picture schedules, demonstrations before unfamiliar tasks, and small-group practice. Give extra response time and check understanding through action. Teach peers how to ask for clarification kindly. Share a brief bilingual strategy sheet with staff after parent consent, using examples that fit arrival, snack, play, and transitions.
- Complete the scheduled audiology evaluation and incorporate its findings into treatment planning. Reassess functional progress using repeated classroom and home probes, including 8/10 direction-following opportunities and message-repair examples. The proposed goals are preliminary and should be adjusted after baseline treatment data. No service outcome is guaranteed by the synthetic score profile.

DEVOLUCIÓN Y FIRMA / FEEDBACK AND SIGNATURE

- Both parents received a Spanish-led explanation with English school terms clarified. Mother stated, “Quiero que pueda contar su día sin que todos adivinen.” Father agreed to practice during vehicle play and meals. The clinician emphasized communication success, patient listening, and continued use of both languages. Parents demonstrated the pause-and-expand strategy before leaving.
- Follow-up contact is planned for 05/19/2025 at 4:30 p.m.. A treatment review is planned for 12 de agosto de 2025. The family may request a translated summary through the clinic contact listed above. Distribution remains limited to the fictional family record unless the parents authorize sharing.
- Electronically signed by Elena Marisol Cárdenas, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, Puente Claro Pediatric Communication Services, on 05/12/2025 at 2:18 p.m.. Record reference: PCP-25-04682. Authorization reference: AUTH-SLP-250506-731. End of fictional assessment report.

Document Type: Pediatric Speech-Language Evaluation / Evaluación de habla y lenguaje
Record Class: Entirely fictional EMR export; instruments, norms, and clinical findings are synthetic
Client Name: María José Valdés Cifuentes
Preferred Name: Marijo
Date of Birth: August 8, 2022
Age at Evaluation: 4;2
Evaluation Date: October 8, 2026
Report Date: October 10, 2026
Appointment Time: 9:15 a.m.–11:05 a.m.
Medical Record Number: BVSL-026184
Medicaid Member Number: 731048269Q
Authorization Number: AUTH-NC-628413
Parent/Guardian: Lucía Valdés and Mateo Cifuentes
Home Address: 2846 Juniper Lantern Lane, Apt. 3B, Briarhaven, North Carolina 27903
County: Mossbridge County
Parent Telephone: (919) 555-0138
Parent Email: lucia.valdes@familymail.example
Preschool: Little Lantern Bilingual Preschool
Referring Physician: Dr. Inés Robledo
Evaluating Clinician: Elena Marisol Duarte, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist
Employer: Puente Claro Pediatric Communication Services
Clinic Telephone: (984) 555-0167
Clinic Website: https://puenteclaro.example
Service Codes: CPT 92523; proposed ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0

Motivo de consulta / Reason for Referral

María José Valdés Cifuentes was referred because family and preschool staff report difficulty understanding longer directions, forming complete messages, and producing clear speech. Her mother, Lucía Valdés, wants help with communication during routines, especially when the child needs assistance or describes something that happened outside the home.

The family described a recent example: “Quiere contar todo, pero se le quedan las palabras. Nosotros esperamos, y a veces ya no quiere hablar.” Her father, Mateo Cifuentes, added that familiar listeners usually understand the general topic, although details require questions. Both parents want the child to keep Spanish while building English for school participation.

The referral asks whether observed difficulties reflect bilingual development, a communication disorder, or both. This evaluation therefore considers skills across languages, exposure history, functional communication, and response to teaching. English performance alone does not determine the clinical impression.

Family priorities include requesting help, answering questions about preschool, joining play, and reducing frustration when listeners misunderstand. The parents also requested practical activities that fit meals, dressing, and shared books without turning home routines into additional homework.

Fuentes de información / Evaluation Procedures

Information came from caregiver interview, developmental history, preschool feedback, direct observation, simulated standardized testing, play samples, and dynamic teaching tasks. The clinician completed the interview and assessment in Spanish and English. The family did not request an interpreter.

For this fictional record, the Bilingual Preschool Language Scale–Third Edition (BPLS-3) and Preschool Speech Sound Inventory–Second Edition (PSSI-2) are invented standardized instruments. Their score conventions and normative results exist only within this synthetic assessment. They do not represent published tests or real normative evidence.

Tasks included picture identification, following directions, sentence completion, story retell, conversation, and speech sampling. Testing alternated languages when the task permitted. Separate language scores appear below, but interpretation emphasizes the combined profile.

The clinician also used a brief teach-and-retest sequence. This examined whether modeling, visual support, and repetition improved learning. Caregiver information describes everyday performance; direct testing describes performance during this visit. These sources were compared rather than treated as interchangeable.

Antecedentes / Developmental and Functional Background

The family first noticed communication concerns when Marijo began combining words. Early messages communicated immediate needs, but longer explanations developed slowly. The mother recalls frequent pointing and bringing objects to adults. Gestures remain useful, especially when the child cannot retrieve a word.

At home, the child participates in dressing, snack preparation, and pretend play. She enjoys toy animals, kitchen sets, and songs with repeated actions. She often starts a familiar activity independently, then seeks an adult when the sequence changes. The family describes her as affectionate, observant, and persistent.

During play with her brother, Diego Cifuentes Valdés, she frequently copies an action before adding language. Her sister, Elena Cifuentes Valdés, sometimes answers for her. The parents have begun asking the sister to wait so the child can attempt her own message.

Reported motor milestones did not raise current concerns. The child walks, runs, uses playground equipment, and manages large puzzle pieces. Fine motor tasks requiring sustained attention are less preferred, although no motor assessment occurred today.

Sleep is generally consistent. Changes in routine can lead to protest, but the family reports no loss of previously acquired communication skills. The child eats a varied household diet and drinks from an open cup with occasional spills. Feeding and swallowing were outside the referral question.

Historia de nacimiento y salud / Birth and Medical History

María José was born at Cedar Lantern Women’s and Children’s Hospital in Briarhaven, North Carolina. Delivery occurred at a gestational age of 35 weeks, 4 days. The mother reported a birth weight of 2.41 kg. Obstetric care was provided by Dr. Adriana Soler.

The infant entered the NICU at Cedar Lantern Women’s and Children’s Hospital for respiratory observation and feeding support. The reported stay lasted 9 days. Neonatologist Dr. Rafael Montalvo followed the infant during that admission. The family reported brief oxygen support and temporary tube feeding, followed by oral feeding before discharge.

These birth details come from caregiver history and the fictional referral summary. The clinician did not independently review a complete neonatal chart. The parents report that the newborn hearing screen was passed before discharge.

Primary care currently occurs at Willowglass Community Pediatric Center with Dr. Inés Robledo. The child has a history of recurrent middle-ear infections. Otolaryngologist Dr. Samuel Pereda placed tympanostomy tubes on February 12, 2025.

Audiologist Nora Beltrán documented hearing responses within the expected range on September 16, 2026. The referral summary reported bilateral responses at 20 dB HL across tested speech frequencies. During today’s visit, the child responded to conversational speech and environmental sounds.

The family reported no seizures, major head injury, or known neurological diagnosis. Seasonal nasal symptoms occur intermittently. Medication information remains with the primary care record. Nothing observed today established a medical cause for the communication findings.

Historia familiar y lingüística / Family and Language History

The household includes both parents and the siblings already described. Spanish is the main language during meals, family calls, discipline, and bedtime. English appears during preschool activities, some books, television, and play with neighborhood children. Exposure varies by person and routine rather than following a fixed schedule.

The mother grew up in Aldea El Cantarito, Guatemala. The maternal grandmother, doña Lupe, still lives at 14 Calle del Guayabo, Barrio Las Luciérnagas, Aldea El Cantarito, Guatemala. The family speaks with her through video calls. She uses Spanish and familiar regional expressions.

A maternal aunt, Rosa Valdés, provides afternoon care. The aunt reported, “Conmigo habla más cuando estamos cocinando; si le hago muchas preguntas, se queda callada.” The family’s occasional babysitter, Teresa Molina, also speaks Spanish. These routines provide meaningful opportunities for conversation.

The father works at Mossbridge Lantern Packaging. He uses English at work and Spanish at home. The mother works at Juniper Hearth Laundry Cooperative and uses both languages with coworkers. Employment names are included only as contextual information about adult language use.

The family dog, Chispa, often joins pretend veterinary play. The child uses short commands during that activity and communicates more readily when an adult follows her lead.

The parents report no diagnosed childhood hearing loss in close relatives. A paternal uncle, Andrés Cifuentes, reportedly received speech services as a child, but details are unavailable. Family history alone does not determine the present diagnosis.

Contexto escolar y apoyos / Educational History

Marijo attends Little Lantern Bilingual Preschool on weekday mornings. Her lead teacher, Miss Ana, uses English for most group instruction and Spanish for selected routines. Classroom assistant la maestra Carmen provides additional Spanish support during transitions and small-group activities.

Teachers report that the child watches peers before starting unfamiliar tasks. She follows familiar classroom routines with visual information. Directions containing several actions often require repetition or demonstration. She contributes more during play than during large-group discussion.

Two classmates, Sofía Méndez and Luis Aranda, frequently invite her into kitchen play. Staff report that she accepts these invitations but sometimes takes an object without explaining what she wants. A classmate, Nico Salvatierra, often guesses her intended message, which helps play continue but can hide communication difficulty.

The classroom uses photographs for daily routines. Staff say these supports improve participation, especially when the schedule changes. Teachers want guidance on prompting without speaking for the child.

The family previously contacted Mossbridge Children’s Development Services Office. Service coordinator Paula Neri completed an intake on September 3, 2026 and provided community referral information. No current IFSP was available for review.

The apartment manager, Mr. Tom, sometimes greets the family in English. The parents report that the child usually waves rather than speaking to him. This isolated behavior was not interpreted as evidence of a social communication disorder.

Observaciones clínicas / Behavior During Assessment

María José entered with her mother and remained near her during the initial interview. She explored toys after the clinician offered a choice and demonstrated an action. Engagement increased when the adult used Spanish, paused, and allowed the child to control part of the play sequence.

The child shared attention by showing objects, looking toward the clinician, and smiling during unexpected events. She accepted turn-taking with familiar materials. She protested removal of a preferred toy, then returned to the task after a visual explanation and a brief movement break.

Testing required several short breaks. Attention was strongest during hands-on activities and weakest during repeated picture questions. The clinician adjusted task order but retained the simulated scoring rules for standardized items.

The child asked for repetition through gaze, gesture, and "¿qué?". She sometimes repeated the last word of a question before answering. This behavior appeared when language demands increased and did not occur consistently across play.

Voice quality was clear during the available sample. No persistent stuttering-like behavior was observed. Oral structures appeared adequate for the speech tasks completed, although this observation does not replace a detailed oral mechanism examination. Participation supported interpretation of the findings, with caution for fatigue and unfamiliar testing demands.

Resultados de pruebas / Score Summary

The following values are simulated clinical data. Standard scores use an invented mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15. Percentiles describe the fictional reference sample only.

| Instrument / Domain | Raw Score | Standard Score | Percentile | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BPLS-3 Spanish Receptive Language | 31 | 78 | 7th percentile | Below expected range |
| BPLS-3 Spanish Expressive Language | 27 | 74 | 4th percentile | Below expected range |
| BPLS-3 English Receptive Language | 24 | 73 | 4th percentile | Exposure-sensitive result |
| BPLS-3 English Expressive Language | 20 | 69 | 2nd percentile | Exposure-sensitive result |
| BPLS-3 Combined Conceptual Language | 58 | 77 | 6th percentile | Cross-language weakness |
| PSSI-2 Speech Sound Production | 42 | 76 | 5th percentile | Reduced speech accuracy |

Lenguaje receptivo y expresivo / Language Findings

Receptive strengths included recognition of familiar objects, common actions, basic body parts, and routine instructions. In Spanish, the child identified pictures across familiar categories with 8/10 accuracy. English performance improved when vocabulary came from preschool routines.

Difficulty increased when directions included location, order, or an unfamiliar verb. The child followed simple directions with 9/10 accuracy but followed directions containing multiple related actions with 4/10 accuracy. Performance increased to 7/10 with mod cues, including gestures and visual choices.

Questions about immediate objects were easier than questions requiring explanation. The child often answered a question about location with an object name. Spanish support improved access to familiar vocabulary, but it did not fully resolve the comprehension difficulty.

Expressive language included short sentences, gestures, and code-switching. During kitchen play, Marijo said "Dame the spoon, para sopa". During animal play, she said "El dog está aquí". These mixed-language messages communicated clear meanings and were not scored as errors merely because they combined languages.

Weaknesses appeared in sentence organization, verb marking, and explaining relationships between events. In Spanish, the child sometimes omitted words needed to clarify who performed an action. In English, limited exposure also affected vocabulary and grammatical forms. The clinician considered these differences separately from weaknesses shared across languages.

During story retell, the child named characters and described visible actions. She needed max cues to explain why a character changed location or how the story ended. With picture support and mod cues, she added a simple sequence.

Dynamic teaching produced improvement. After modeling, the child used a newly taught action word in 6/8 opportunities. She retained the word after a play break in 3/4 opportunities. Sentence expansion remained inconsistent without support. This pattern suggests learning capacity alongside a need for structured language intervention.

Habla, muestra lingüística y comunicación social

Speech errors affected intelligibility in both languages. The child replaced some velar sounds with sounds produced farther forward in the mouth. For example, /k/ was sometimes realized as [t]. The target "casa" was produced as "tasa", and the target "cookie" was produced as "tootie".

Some consonant clusters were reduced. The target "plato" was produced as "pato". Liquid production varied by word and language. English /ɹ/ was sometimes realized as [w], although this finding alone did not determine severity.

The clinician observed inconsistent loss of unstressed syllables in longer words. Errors increased during connected speech and when the child attempted unfamiliar vocabulary. Familiar words were clearer. Productions did not show a consistent pattern of disrupted prosody or effortful transitions during this sample.

An unfamiliar listener understood approximately 65% of connected speech in the room. The mother understood approximately 85% within familiar topics. These estimates reflect the available sample and listener context.

A bilingual language sample contained 50 spontaneous utterances. Selected productions included "Yo quiere ese", "Se cayó porque boom", and "I no find it". The fictional SALT-style transcription included [EW] for an extra word and [EU] for an utterance-level error. These codes are transcription markers, not identifiers.

Social communication strengths included shared enjoyment, functional gestures, seeking help, and interest in peers. The child repaired some misunderstandings by pointing or showing an object. Verbal repair was less effective when the listener needed details.

During pretend shopping, the child greeted the clinician, exchanged objects, and followed a familiar play script. When the script changed, she watched and copied before contributing. This appeared related to language demands and task familiarity.

The child used eye gaze naturally with gestures and speech. She noticed when the adult acted confused, but often repeated the same message. With a model, she added information or selected another word.

Caregiver and teacher reports agree that communication is strongest with familiar people and predictable activities. There is insufficient evidence from this visit to infer a separate social communication diagnosis. Continued observation across classroom activities will help clarify participation needs.

Impresiones clínicas / Clinical Impressions

The fictional findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder. Proposed diagnostic codes are ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0. The child shows difficulty understanding complex language, organizing messages, and maintaining clear speech across languages and settings.

Bilingual exposure explains some uneven vocabulary and grammatical performance. It does not fully explain the weaknesses observed in Spanish, the combined conceptual score, caregiver examples, and supported narrative tasks. The clinical impression rests on these converging findings rather than on low English scores alone.

Communication difficulty affects requesting assistance, explaining events, following classroom directions, and entering peer play. Frustration appears greatest when adults ask repeated questions before recognizing the intended message.

The child also demonstrates important strengths. She seeks interaction, uses gestures, learns from models, and benefits from visual information. Family involvement and bilingual classroom support provide useful foundations for intervention.

Interpretation remains limited by a single visit, variable attention, and incomplete historical records. The score table contains invented normative data and cannot support decisions about any real child. Within this synthetic case, functional findings provide the clearest basis for the recommendations.

The clinician discussed the results with Lucía Valdés in Spanish. The mother summarized her understanding: “Entonces seguimos con español, y le damos tiempo para explicar.” The clinician affirmed continued use of the family’s strongest language.

Recomendaciones / Plan de intervención

1. Begin bilingual speech-language intervention through Puente Claro Pediatric Communication Services. The proposed schedule is one 45-minute session weekly for an initial block of 12 weeks. Adjust frequency after reviewing participation, progress, and family priorities.

2. Target comprehension within daily routines. Present a short direction, pause, and check the child’s action before repeating. Add a gesture or picture when needed. Practice location and sequence concepts with real objects before using worksheet-style tasks.

3. Expand the child’s messages without requiring immediate repetition. If Marijo says "perro aquí", model "El perro está aquí". Keep the response connected to her meaning. Use Spanish or English according to the activity and the adult’s comfort.

4. Teach communication repair during play. Model "Ayúdame", "I mean this one", and "Te enseño". Accept pointing while helping the child add useful words. Praise successful clarification rather than speech length alone.

5. Address speech patterns that affect intelligibility across languages. Begin with functional words containing /k/ and /g/, then examine cluster targets. Use short practice periods with meaningful play. Record cueing needs and generalization outside imitation.

6. Support story language with photographs or a simple picture sequence. Ask what happened first, what changed, and how the event ended. Offer a model when the child cannot answer. Avoid turning every shared book into a series of test questions.

7. Continue Spanish at home. Encourage natural conversation with doña Lupe and other familiar relatives. English practice can occur through preschool routines and enjoyable shared activities. Neither language needs to replace the other.

8. Coordinate with Miss Ana and la maestra Carmen after caregiver authorization. Recommend visual directions, additional response time, and small-group opportunities. Adults should check the intended message before correcting speech.

9. Encourage supported play with Sofía Méndez and Luis Aranda. Provide a shared activity and simple language models. Give the child a chance to request, comment, and solve a small problem without a peer answering first.

10. Maintain hearing follow-up as directed by Dr. Samuel Pereda and the primary care physician. If new hearing concerns arise, request audiology review. Refer additional developmental questions through the child’s usual medical team.

Objetivos iniciales y seguimiento / Follow-Up

Initial goals will address functional directions, sentence expansion, verbal repair, and speech clarity. Establish a baseline during the first treatment visits using familiar activities in both languages.

A proposed comprehension goal is completion of related directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. A proposed expressive goal is production of an expanded message in 80% of structured play opportunities with mod cues. A speech goal will measure selected sound patterns in functional words after stimulability testing.

Review progress on January 7, 2027. Compare clinic performance with caregiver examples and classroom participation. Repeat standardized testing only when the interval and clinical question support it.

Caregiver education occurred before departure at 11:05 a.m.. The mother received a written summary in English with Spanish explanations. She reported agreement with the proposed plan.

Electronically Signed By: Elena Marisol Duarte, MS, CCC-SLP
Signature Date: October 10, 2026
Signature Time: 2:40 p.m.
Provider Record ID: SLP-NC-SYN-48271
Next Scheduled Visit: October 15, 2026 at 10:00 a.m.
