text:
BILINGUAL PEDIATRIC SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION  
Evaluación del habla y lenguaje

Document status: Fictional clinical report for offline software testing.

Client: Mateo Julián Valverde  
Preferred name: Teo  
Date of birth: 01/03/2021  
Age at evaluation: 4;2  
Evaluation date: 3 de marzo de 2025  
Electronic encounter date: 2025-03-03  
Session time: 9:15 a.m.–10:45 a.m.  
Parent/guardian: Elena Valverde  
Other parent: Gabriel Valverde  
Home address: 284 Lantern Finch Lane, Cedarlune, North Carolina 28763  
Telephone: (919) 555-0148  
Parent email: elena.valverde@example.com  
Record number: SLP-250303-047  
Medicaid identification: 482761935Q  
Authorization number: AUTH-2502-1186  
School: Juniper Lantern Preschool  
Referring physician: Dr. Amalia Serrano  
Evaluator: Inés Marisol Duarte, MS, CCC-SLP  
Employer: Willow Lantern Pediatric Communication  
Practice website: https://willowlantern.example.com  
Service location: 61 Meadowglass Court, Cedarlune, North Carolina 28763  
Procedure: CPT 92523

1. REASON FOR REFERRAL / MOTIVO DE CONSULTA

1.1 Presenting concerns

Mateo was referred for a bilingual assessment because his family and preschool staff reported difficulty understanding connected speech. They also described short spoken messages, difficulty answering questions, and frustration when listeners requested clarification. His mother, Elena Valverde, stated, “En casa entiende mucho, pero cuando quiere contar algo, se queda buscando las palabras.”

The referral requested evaluation across Spanish and English. The purpose was to examine communication skills, language exposure, functional participation, and possible treatment needs. This report considers both languages together while documenting differences between contexts.

1.2 Family priorities

The family wants Mateo to explain what happened during preschool, ask for help, and communicate during play without abandoning his message. His father, Gabriel Valverde, added, “Queremos que pueda hablar con sus abuelos y también con los niños de la escuela.”

The parents identified successful communication as their main priority. They did not request elimination of Spanish, changes to family language practices, or correction of bilingual code-switching.

2. BACKGROUND / ANTECEDENTES

2.1 Educational history

Mateo attends Juniper Lantern Preschool on weekday mornings. His lead teacher, Ms. Nadia Flores, completed a classroom questionnaire on 02/24/2025. The classroom assistant, Mr. Evan Bellamy, provided examples of communication during snack and outdoor play.

Staff reported that he follows familiar classroom routines with visual support. Novel directions often require repetition or demonstration. During group discussion, he usually contributes a brief phrase after another child speaks. He participates more readily when an adult offers choices.

Previously, he attended Little Acorn Harbor Daycare. Records from that setting described interest in books and construction toys, with limited verbal explanations during peer conflict.

2.2 Previous services

A developmental intake occurred through Larkmere County Child Development Services Agency on el martes 4 de junio de 2024. Service coordinator Camila Ortez recommended further assessment. The family reported no previous individual speech-language treatment.

A prior occupational therapy consultation with Jonah Mireles addressed transitions and participation. No ongoing occupational therapy was reported.

3. BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY / NACIMIENTO Y SALUD

3.1 Birth history

According to maternal report, Mateo was born on January 3, 2021 at Meadowglass Regional Birth Center in Cedarlune, North Carolina. Pregnancy was described as uncomplicated. Delivery occurred at term, and the family reported no neonatal intensive care admission.

His mother recalled feeding fatigue during the first weeks, followed by improved feeding without specialized intervention. No birth records were available for independent review. Therefore, these details remain caregiver-reported history.

3.2 Medical and hearing history

The family reported recurrent ear infections during early childhood. An audiology visit at Larkmere Children's Hearing Center on 11/18/2024 reportedly found hearing adequate for speech access. The written audiology report was reviewed and documented bilateral responses within the clinic's expected screening range.

Dr. Amalia Serrano reported no current neurological diagnosis. The family denied swallowing concerns, seizures, or recent hospitalization. Occasional seasonal congestion was reported. During this assessment, breathing appeared comfortable, and no persistent voice concern was observed.

Sleep and appetite were described as stable. Medical information was considered as context rather than as an explanation for the communication findings.

4. FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY / FAMILIA E IDIOMAS

4.1 Household and caregivers

Mateo lives with both parents and his older sister, Luz Valverde, age 7;6. His maternal grandmother, Beatriz Nolasco, provides afternoon care twice weekly. A babysitter, Marina Cordero, assists on occasional evenings.

His mother works at Copper Fern Packaging. His father works at Lantern Ridge Bicycle Works. The household is located in Larkmere County.

The family described regular contact with cousins Dalia Nolasco and Nico Nolasco. Their dog, Canela, frequently appears in the child's stories and pretend play. The family reported that talking about the pet often increases his willingness to communicate.

4.2 Language exposure

Spanish has been present since birth. English exposure increased through daycare and preschool. His mother and grandmother primarily use Spanish. His father uses both languages. His sister, Luz, often starts play in English and switches to Spanish during family routines.

The parents estimated current exposure as 60% Spanish and 40% English across a typical week. These estimates describe exposure, not language proficiency.

His mother explained, “Cuando está cansado, pide todo en español; cuando juega a los superhéroes, sale más inglés.” The clinician observed similar switching. Bilingual responses were accepted throughout testing when permitted by the task. Language difference alone was not treated as evidence of impairment.

5. ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES / PROCEDIMIENTOS

5.1 Measures and sources

Assessment included caregiver interview, teacher questionnaires, record review, structured play, oral mechanism observation, and bilingual language sampling. The Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish was administered using its bilingual procedures. The PLS-5 Spanish provided the standardized language scores reported below.

Selected picture prompts from the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation–Third Edition supported descriptive examination of English speech sounds. Administration was modified for bilingual sampling. Consequently, no standardized articulation score was calculated.

Conversational samples were examined using Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts conventions. Relevant SALT annotations included [EW] for selected word-level errors and [EU] for utterance-level errors.

5.2 Participation and validity

Mateo separated from his parent after a brief play routine. He benefited from a visual schedule, movement breaks, and predictable task endings. Standardized items followed permitted administration procedures; additional teaching occurred afterward.

Attention varied during longer verbal tasks. The findings are considered a reasonable estimate of performance that day, with bilingual experience and caregiver information incorporated into interpretation. They do not establish a fixed limit on future learning.

6. TEST RESULTS / RESULTADOS

6.1 Score table

| Measure | Domain or task | Score | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish | Auditory Comprehension | Standard score 83; percentile 13 | Below the expected range |
| PLS-5 Spanish | Expressive Communication | Standard score 81; percentile 10 | Below the expected range |
| PLS-5 Spanish | Total Language | Standard score 80; percentile 9 | Below the expected range |
| Bilingual criterion task | Familiar one-step directions | 8/10; 80% | Stronger with familiar vocabulary |
| Bilingual criterion task | Two-part directions | 4/10; 40% | Reduced accuracy without demonstration |
| Dynamic learning task | Novel word identification after teaching | 7/10; 70% | Improvement with mediated practice |
| Connected speech sample | Estimated intelligibility to clinician | 65% | Context improved understanding |

6.2 Receptive language

Mateo identified familiar objects, actions, and common body parts. He understood routine requests in either language when the situation provided clear clues. Spanish responses were more consistent for household vocabulary; English responses were stronger for several classroom routines.

Difficulty increased with unfamiliar spatial concepts, longer directions, and questions requiring relationships between events. For example, he located an item placed on a table but needed demonstration when asked to position it behind another object.

During teaching, accuracy improved with gesture, contrastive examples, and mod cues. He retained several newly taught words during a delayed play activity. This response supports the use of structured teaching while leaving open the need to measure learning across repeated sessions.

6.3 Expressive language

Spontaneous messages usually contained brief combinations of words. Longer messages occurred during familiar pretend play but often omitted information needed by an unfamiliar listener. Vocabulary was distributed across languages rather than contained entirely within either language.

Observed productions included "yo quiero carro", "he go casa", and "más big one". These examples show code-switching and developing sentence structure. Code-switching itself was not scored as an error.

Separate concerns included limited elaboration, inconsistent verb marking within each language, and difficulty forming complete explanations. When prompted about a classroom event, he named objects but did not independently describe the sequence. With picture support and mod cues, he added an action and a location.

7. SPEECH SOUND AND ORAL MECHANISM FINDINGS / HABLA

7.1 Speech production

Speech sampling showed reduced accuracy for velar sounds, consonant clusters, and some word-final consonants. The target /k/ was sometimes produced as [t], particularly in longer words. The target /g/ showed a similar forward placement pattern.

During imitation, the target "casa" was produced as "tasa". The English target "school" was produced as "cool". A glide substitution, [w], occurred in some English words containing /ɹ/. That finding was interpreted within developmental and bilingual context.

Patterns were examined across both languages. Differences attributable to Spanish phonology were distinguished from patterns that reduced clarity in both languages. The combined effect of several patterns, message length, and reduced repair skills limited conversational intelligibility.

7.2 Stimulability and oral observations

Mateo produced /k/ in isolation with max cues and achieved 6/10 accurate attempts after practice. Accuracy decreased in syllables and connected speech.

Facial symmetry, lip movement, and tongue movement appeared adequate for the observed tasks. No structural concern was identified through this limited examination. Diadochokinetic tasks were not interpreted because participation was inconsistent. Voice and fluency did not present a primary concern during the sample.

8. SOCIAL COMMUNICATION AND PLAY / COMUNICACIÓN SOCIAL

8.1 Interaction

Mateo initiated shared play, showed toys to adults, and checked listeners' reactions. He used pointing and facial expression effectively. When misunderstood, he sometimes repeated the same phrase louder rather than changing the message.

His teacher described successful play with classmates Mila Rentería and Owen Calder. Communication was harder when classmate Tessa Mora changed the game rules quickly. These observations suggest that language demands affected participation.

8.2 Narrative and repair

A picture sequence about a lost toy elicited labels and isolated actions. He needed direct support to identify the problem and explain the ending. After modeling, he used "first", "then", and "al final", with mod cues.

During pretend veterinary play involving Canela, he sustained interaction longer and offered more spontaneous language. This familiar theme may provide a useful starting point for treatment.

9. IMPRESSIONS / IMPRESIÓN CLÍNICA

9.1 Clinical interpretation

Findings indicate receptive and expressive language weaknesses affecting participation across Spanish and English. Standardized results, functional observations, caregiver concerns, and teacher reports support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder. The proposed diagnostic code is ICD-10 F80.2.

Speech sound patterns also reduced intelligibility beyond the effects of language choice alone. The proposed speech sound diagnosis is ICD-10 F80.0. Conclusions should be reviewed as treatment provides additional samples.

Bilingual exposure does not explain all observed difficulties. At the same time, this evaluation does not support reducing Spanish use. Family language remains central to relationships, learning, and communication.

9.2 Strengths and limitations

Strengths include social interest, pretend play, gesture use, and improvement with teaching. Limitations include a single assessment session, variable attention, and incomplete early medical records. Classroom observation would help confirm how these findings affect daily routines.

10. RECOMMENDATIONS / RECOMENDACIONES

10.1 Intervention plan

1. Begin bilingual speech-language treatment targeting comprehension, sentence expansion, speech clarity, and communication repair.
2. Use Spanish and English according to the activity, family priorities, and the child's available vocabulary.
3. Pair spoken directions with pictures or gestures, then reduce support as accuracy improves.
4. Practice selected speech targets in meaningful words before increasing phrase length.
5. Teach repair strategies through modeling, choices, and supported practice.
6. Coordinate classroom supports with Ms. Nadia Flores and the family.

10.2 Initial functional targets

Treatment should address following two-part directions, describing actions with sufficient detail, and answering simple questions about recent events. Suggested criteria include 8/10 successful opportunities across repeated sessions, with support reduced toward min cues.

Speech practice should begin with stimulable targets, including /k/, and monitor generalization across languages. Targets should reflect functional words rather than accent modification.

10.3 Home practice and follow-up

Caregivers can expand a short message by adding one useful detail, then allow time for a response. Durante la lectura, pause and invite a comment instead of asking continuous questions. Accept mixed-language responses.

A planning call is scheduled for 03.10.2025 at 4:30 p.m.. Progress review is proposed for June 3, 2025. The family received this report on 05/03/2025, documented in day/month/year format.

Prepared by Inés Marisol Duarte, MS, CCC-SLP

IFSP REVIEW / REVISIÓN DEL PLAN FAMILIAR

- This fictional North Carolina infant-toddler record documents a family-centered IFSP review held on October 8, 2026. The meeting occurred at home, with video participation available. The family selected English and Spanish for discussion, written summaries, and coaching.
- The review concerns Emilio Rafael Castañeda, called Milo at home. His birth date is June 2, 2024, and his chronological age is 2;4. The next review is scheduled for January 7, 2027.
- The bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, Marisol Elena Varela, prepared this record through Little Lantern Pediatric Communication Services. The family reviewed the meaning of each outcome before agreeing to the plan. Spanish comments reflect family wording, with permission to include them.

INFORMACIÓN DE LA FAMILIA / FAMILY INFORMATION

- The child lives with his mother, Lucía Castañeda, his father, Andrés Beltrán, and his sister, Inés Beltrán. His sister is 6 years old. Both parents participate in decisions and authorize routine communication with the providers listed in this plan.
- The home address is 418 Willow Lantern Lane, apartment 3B, Larkwell, NC 27997, in Fernwater County. The family prefers home visits because transportation arrangements change weekly. Parking is available beside the building; visitors should use the side entrance.
- The primary telephone number is 252-555-0147. The alternate telephone number is 252-555-0183. The preferred email is lucia.castaneda@example.com. The family requests Spanish voicemail messages and short English text reminders. Staff must confirm the recipient before discussing service details.

FAMILY CONNECTIONS / NUESTRA GENTE

- The maternal grandmother, doña Lupe, provides care on two afternoons each week. An aunt, Beatriz Salcedo, helps with appointments. The family calls the babysitter, Nora Quiñones, when work schedules overlap. Each caregiver uses Spanish during meals, songs, and play.
- The grandmother’s mailing address is Calle de las Luciérnagas 27, El Pueblito de las Jacarandas, near San Lucero, Mexico. Relatives describe this village as their hometown. Video calls support family relationships; the parents want communication strategies that work during these calls.
- The family’s dog, Canela, often joins floor play. The child enjoys bringing the dog’s bowl to an adult. A neighbor, Mr. Tom, sometimes offers transportation. He does not receive clinical records or participate in service decisions.

COORDINACIÓN DE SERVICIOS / SERVICE COORDINATION

- The assigned service coordinator is Elena Mercado at Fernwater River CDSA Office. Her telephone number is 252-555-0126, and her email is elena.mercado@example.com. She will organize reviews, explain available supports, and help the family track referrals.
- The CDSA record number is FW-CDSA-260184. The IFSP authorization number is IFSP-261008-73. The Medicaid member number is 834729516L. These fictional identifiers appear here to support testing; providers must use the correct record when documenting visits.
- The service coordinator will contact the family monthly and after any missed visit requiring rescheduling. The family prefers calls after 4:15 p.m.. Routine messages should state the purpose, the requested response, and the deadline in clear language.

PARTICIPANTES / REVIEW PARTICIPANTS

- The review included both parents, the service coordinator, and the bilingual speech-language pathologist. Interpreter Daniela Rosales supported discussion of administrative forms. The clinician conducted communication coaching directly in both languages and checked understanding through family explanations.
- Occupational therapist Owen Paredes joined by video. Physical therapist Tessa Molina provided a written update dated October 5, 2026. Pediatrician Dr. Nadia Serrano sent the most recent developmental summary with family authorization.
- Classroom teacher Miss Ana and assistant teacher la maestra Carmen contributed routine observations. Their comments addressed participation during snacks, arrival, and outdoor play. The family requested practical examples instead of long lists of developmental terms.

PREOCUPACIONES / FAMILY CONCERNS

- The mother said, “Yo sé que entiende muchas cosas, pero cuando quiere algo se desespera. I want him to tell us before he cries.” She described the hardest moments as opening snacks, leaving the playground, and waiting while another person prepares food.
- The father said, “No queremos quitarle el español. En casa hablamos español, and at daycare he hears more English.” Both parents want the child to communicate with relatives and classroom adults without treating either language as a problem.
- The grandmother said, “Cuando yo no entiendo, me lleva de la mano. Quiero que pueda decirme qué necesita.” The family identified repeated guessing as tiring. They want gestures, pictures, and words to work together, especially when spoken messages are unclear.

PRIORIDADES / WHAT MATTERS FIRST

- The family selected three immediate priorities: requesting help during meals, joining familiar play, and moving between activities with less distress. The parents want changes that fit existing routines. They do not want separate homework sessions or pressure to repeat words.
- The mother added, “Primero que pueda pedir, después veremos las frases.” The father wants everyone to respond consistently when the child points, signs, or speaks. Caregivers agreed to pause briefly, notice the message, and offer a useful spoken model.
- The family values shared meals, bedtime songs, weekend visits, and respectful participation in church gatherings. They define progress as easier daily communication. They also want the child to enjoy people, make choices, and ask for a break when needed.

FORTALEZAS / CHILD AND FAMILY STRENGTHS

- Emilio seeks familiar adults, brings interesting objects to them, and laughs during predictable games. He notices changes in songs and sometimes supplies the final sound. He follows familiar directions more readily when adults show the object or action.
- The family already uses expressive gestures, repeated songs, and patient turn-taking. The sister offers toys and waits for a response. Caregivers notice small communication changes and share examples across households. These strengths provide several natural opportunities for practice each day.
- Interests include toy buses, bubbles, animal figures, water play, and looking through family photographs. Preferred activities can support interaction without requiring new materials. The team will follow the child’s choices while adding manageable communication opportunities.

RUTINAS DIARIAS / DAILY ROUTINES

- Breakfast usually begins at 7:20 a.m.. The child chooses between two familiar foods by reaching or pointing. Adults sometimes anticipate the choice immediately. Coaching will help caregivers show both choices, wait, and respond to the first clear message.
- Dressing happens near the couch before departure. The child participates by lifting his arms and finding shoes. Waiting for a zipper often leads to frustration. The family will pair a gesture with “help” or “ayuda” and assist promptly.
- Evening routines include dinner, bath, quiet play, and a song around 7:45 p.m.. The family reports that communication improves when the room is calm. Providers will use these predictable activities for practice and avoid adding demands when the child is tired.

CHILDCARE AND SCHOOL / CUIDADO Y ESCUELA

- The child attends Willow Nest Family Daycare three mornings weekly. The classroom also receives support through Fernwater Early Head Start Partnership. Arrival includes greeting an adult, storing a bag, and selecting an activity. Visual choices are available beside the play shelf.
- Classmates Alma Torres and Jonah Wells often join bus play. The child watches their actions and occasionally offers a vehicle. Staff will support short exchanges without requiring spoken greetings. Adults will acknowledge looking, giving, pointing, and vocalizing as participation.
- The sister attends Lantern Grove Primary School. The parents want home strategies that fit the family’s afternoon schedule. Teachers will share one useful example weekly, including the routine, the adult response, and whether the child needed additional support.

OTRAS AGENCIAS / COMMUNITY SUPPORTS

- Fernwater County DSS Family Support Unit assists with transportation planning. Larkwell WIC Nutrition Office provides nutrition appointments. Fernwater Smart Start Family Resource Center offers playgroup information. The service coordinator will check referral status with the family before contacting these agencies.
- The father works at Riverglass Bicycle Assembly, and the mother works at Juniper Basket Packing House. Rotating shifts affect appointment availability. The family requests advance scheduling and wants missed visits discussed without assuming that reduced attendance means reduced interest.
- The family received pediatric care at Larkwell Children’s Community Hospital. A hearing follow-up is scheduled for October 22, 2026. The family resource page is https://fernwater-family.example.com/support. No agency may share this IFSP beyond the agreed recipients without appropriate authorization.

EVALUACIÓN / COMMUNICATION SUMMARY

- The bilingual evaluation occurred on September 24, 2026. Tasks included caregiver interview, play observation, and selected activities from Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish. Fictional results included Auditory Comprehension standard score 82, Expressive Communication standard score 76, and Total Language standard score 78.
- The corresponding reported rankings were 12th percentile, 5th percentile, and 7th percentile. The team considered these results alongside participation across both languages. The scores describe this assessment session and do not replace information about communication in familiar routines.
- During a brief language sample, the child produced “ma”, “agua”, “go”, and “más”. The sample included [EW] on one attempted word. Productions varied with activity and listener familiarity. Caregiver reports identified additional words that did not occur during observation.

HALLAZGOS FUNCIONALES / FUNCTIONAL FINDINGS

- The child communicated an intentional request in 6/10 observed opportunities when objects were visible. He used a gesture with a vocalization in 3/10 opportunities. Adults understood familiar requests more readily than messages about missing objects or unexpected events.
- Speech observations included emerging /m/, /p/, and /b/. One attempted word contained [w] where the adult model contained /l/. The team will prioritize useful messages and comfortable participation while monitoring speech patterns across languages.
- The occupational therapist reported difficulty waiting during dressing and cleaning hands. The physical therapist reported improving balance during floor-to-standing transitions. The pediatrician documented ICD-10 F80.2 for communication services. The speech evaluation used CPT 92523; planned treatment uses CPT 92507.

RESULTADO UNO / REQUESTING HELP AND CHOICES

- Outcome: During meals, dressing, and play, Milo will communicate a choice, request, or need for help using a gesture, picture, word, or combined message. The family wants to understand him before frustration interrupts the activity.
- Strategies: Adults will offer two meaningful choices, hold items where they can be seen, and wait briefly. They will model “more”, “más”, “open”, “abre”, “help”, or “ayuda” as the situation requires. Adults will accept approximations and provide the requested assistance.
- Measurement: Caregivers will record success in 8/10 opportunities across three routines, with no more than min cues, for two consecutive weeks. The starting level is 6/10 with mod cues. The review will consider caregiver observations and direct coaching examples.

RESULTADO DOS / SHARED PLAY AND CONNECTION

- Outcome: During familiar play, the child will complete at least three back-and-forth exchanges with an adult or peer. Exchanges may include giving an object, copying an action, looking toward a partner, making a sound, or using a word.
- Strategies: Adults will join bus and animal play, copy the child’s action, and add one small change. They will model “my turn”, “mi turno”, “go”, and “va” when useful. The sister may participate voluntarily; adults will manage materials and waiting.
- Measurement: The family and classroom staff will identify successful exchanges in 4/5 familiar play opportunities with min cues. The baseline is one exchange in 2/5 opportunities with mod cues. Partners will stop or simplify the activity when the child signals discomfort.

RESULTADO TRES / TRANSITIONS AND PARTICIPATION

- Outcome: During departure, handwashing, and bedtime, the child will communicate readiness, refusal, or a request for support and complete the transition with an adult. The family wants predictable steps and fewer episodes of prolonged crying.
- Strategies: Adults will use a simple picture sequence, show the next object, and give a brief warning. They will model “all done”, “terminé”, “wait”, and “espera”. Caregivers will acknowledge protest and offer a manageable choice whenever the routine allows.
- Measurement: Success means completing the transition with a usable message in 80% of recorded opportunities across two weeks, with mod cues or less. The starting estimate is 40%. Caregivers will record what helped, including reduced noise, extra time, or physical assistance.

PLAN DE SERVICIOS / SERVICE DATES

- Speech-language services begin on October 12, 2026 and continue through January 7, 2027. Frequency is one 45-minute visit weekly in the home or daycare. The bilingual clinician will coach caregivers, observe routines, and coordinate communication strategies with classroom staff.
- Occupational therapy continues from October 15, 2026 through January 7, 2027, twice monthly for 45 minutes at home. Physical therapy consultation continues from October 20, 2026 through January 7, 2027, monthly for 30 minutes in a familiar play setting.
- Service coordination continues throughout the review period, with monthly contact and additional support as needed. The interpreter attends administrative discussions when requested. Providers will arrange replacement visits within available schedules and document cancellations, family preferences, and changes in setting.

COACHING / APOYO ENTRE VISITAS

- Each speech visit will begin with the family’s current concern and one recent success. The clinician will observe a selected routine, demonstrate a strategy if useful, and invite the caregiver to try it. The family will choose what to practice between visits.
- The mother said, “Si me das una idea para la comida, sí la puedo hacer. Muchas hojas, no.” The team agreed to provide one short bilingual note after each visit. Photos of household objects may support choices when the family prefers them.
- The father said, “Quiero aprender cómo esperar sin dejarlo llorando.” Coaching will distinguish a brief communication pause from withholding needed care. Adults will respond promptly to distress and adapt expectations. Food, comfort, and access to help remain available throughout practice.

SEGUIMIENTO / REVIEW AND FAMILY AGREEMENT

- The service coordinator will check the hearing appointment result and transportation plan by October 29, 2026. The clinician will compare home and classroom examples at the next monthly contact. Changes in hearing information, attendance, or family priorities may require an earlier review.
- Progress notes will identify the routine, the child’s message, the adult strategy, and the support needed. The family may share examples verbally instead of completing forms. Providers will review patterns across settings and languages before changing outcomes or service frequency.
- Both parents stated that the outcomes reflect their priorities. The mother said, “Así sí se parece a nuestra vida.” The family received a bilingual summary on October 8, 2026. The clinician, Marisol Elena Varela, documented agreement and routed the review to the service coordinator.

Información familiar / Family information

I completed this review in Spanish and English according to each participant’s preference. Mother preferred Spanish for planning and English for written appointment reminders. Father used both languages. The family requested one combined document so both parents can share the same strategies.

Tadeo lives with his parents and sister, Luz Marín Cevallos, age 5;1. His maternal grandmother, Belisa Cevallos, provides care during overlapping work shifts. The family’s dog, Miga, often stays beside the play mat. Mother works at Lantern Loom Packaging Cooperative. Father works at Cedarwheel Equipment Repair. Their schedules change weekly.

Preocupaciones y prioridades / Family’s own words

Mother said, “Quiero que Teo me diga qué necesita, aunque sea con sus manos primero. When he cries, yo adivino, and sometimes I get it wrong.”

Father said, “He understands our routines, pero cuando cambiamos algo se frustra. I want him to ask for help before he throws the cup.”

Grandmother said, “En español platica más conmigo. No quiero que pierda eso cuando empiece más inglés.” I explained that intervention will support communication across both languages. The family does not need to stop speaking Spanish at home.

The parents ranked priorities as requesting help, joining meals without prolonged distress, and communicating with familiar children. Mother added, “No necesitamos palabras perfectas; necesitamos entendernos.”

The family identified shared meals, music, and bedtime stories as strengths. They prefer strategies that fit existing routines. They declined an additional separate practice period because both parents already manage changing shifts and transportation.

Rutinas diarias / What the day looks like

Breakfast usually begins at 7:30 a.m.. Tadeo reaches toward food and sometimes leads an adult to the refrigerator. Adults can offer two visible choices before opening packages. The family wants fewer rapid questions during meals.

On childcare mornings, departure occurs around 8:20 a.m.. Teo attends Little Lantern Bilingual Playhouse three mornings weekly. Ms. Nadia Peralta reports that he joins songs and watches peers before approaching them. Classmate Amaro Vélez offers toy vehicles. Another child, Mina Corbel, participates in the same snack group.

After pickup, grandmother offers lunch and quiet play. Sister Luz attends Juniper Kite Primary School and joins afternoon play when she returns.

Bath time starts near 6:40 p.m.. Bedtime books begin around 7:45 p.m.. Mother reported, “La luz bajita helps him settle.” Here, luz describes the room lighting.

Agencias y apoyos / Other services

Lunavale Riverbend CDSA coordinates the IFSP and monitors access. Copper Finch County WIC Office provides nutrition appointments. Copper Finch Family Connections assists with transportation requests. Dispatcher Oren Bellwick is the family’s listed transportation contact.

Pediatrician Dr. Tessa Quintero practices at Juniper Harbor Children’s Hospital. The family reported a hearing appointment on 05-22-2025; the written result was unavailable today. The coordinator will request it with the existing release.

No additional therapy was reported. Mother recalled the first developmental concern “el martes 4 de junio de 2024, cuando dejó de intentar algunas palabras.” That statement is family history, not a verified finding. The pediatrician’s referral is dated 2025-02-18.

Resumen clínico bilingüe / Review findings

During the home observation, Tadeo communicated through pointing, reaching, vocalizations, and several spoken forms. He followed familiar directions more consistently when adults included gestures. Communication varied with the activity, listener, and available visual support.

The evaluation dated 06/03/2025 included Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish). The record lists Auditory Comprehension standard score 79, 8th percentile; Expressive Communication standard score 75, 5th percentile; and Total Language standard score 76, 5th percentile. These findings support the functional observations but do not describe every bilingual skill.

A brief language sample included "ma agua", "no", and "go". One modeled utterance carried the SALT code [EW]. Speech included /m/, /p/, and [w]. Intelligibility was approximately 40% to an unfamiliar listener in this sample.

The working diagnosis remains F80.2. Treatment planning emphasizes participation, caregiver coaching, and communication across languages.

Resultados y estrategias / Functional outcomes

Outcome 1: Request help during meals and play.

By 12/16/2025, Teo will request an item or help using a gesture, picture, sign, or spoken form in 8/10 opportunities across meals and play, with min cues, during three consecutive caregiver checks.

Adults will place desired items within view, pause, and acknowledge any clear communication attempt. They may model "ayuda", "help", "más", or "more" once, then wait. Adults will honor the request without requiring repetition.

Current performance was 3/10 opportunities with mod cues. Mother will record a small sample twice weekly. Father will use the same approach during weekend breakfast.

Outcome 2: Participate in a predictable meal routine.

By 12/16/2025, Tadeo will use a communication signal to choose food, request a pause, or indicate completion during 80% of observed meals across two weeks, with min verbal cues.

The family will use a simple first-then picture sequence and offer two choices. Adults will model "terminé", "all done", and "descanso" without turning the meal into a drill. Distress will prompt a pause and support.

Baseline participation was 2/5 sampled meals, based on caregiver notes. Grandmother said, “Podemos esperar un poquito; no tenemos que preguntar todo seguido.” The clinician will coach pacing during an actual meal.

Outcome 3: Join a short exchange with another child.

By 12/16/2025, Teo will complete three turns in a shared activity with a sibling or peer in 4/5 opportunities, using actions, gestures, or words, with mod cues or less.

Adults will start with rolling a ball, parking cars, or passing puzzle pieces. Ms. Peralta will offer a familiar partner and model "mi turno" or "your turn". Sister Luz can join when she chooses; she is not responsible for therapy.

Current performance was 1/5 opportunities. The family and childcare staff will share brief observations about successful activities and supports.

Servicios / Service plan and dates

Speech-language services will begin 06/17/2025 and continue through 12/16/2025, once weekly for 45 minutes. Service code: CPT 92507. The primary setting is the home. One monthly visit may occur at childcare when the family and classroom agree.

Celina Arvelo will provide bilingual caregiver coaching through Firefly Bridge Pediatric Therapy, PLLC. Sessions will include observation, joint practice, reflection, and one manageable strategy for the coming week.

Mariela Voss will provide monthly coordination and contact the family sooner if access changes. The next coordination call is scheduled for 07/02/2025 at 12:15 p.m.. The next formal review is planned for 12/09/2025.

The coordinator will begin transition planning before the child’s third birthday. The family prefers a joint call with both parents.

Acuerdos / Family participation and follow-up

Both parents agreed that these outcomes reflect their priorities. Mother said, “Sí, así funciona para nosotros. Spanish at home, English cuando hace falta, and everybody can help.”

The family received an explanation of voluntary participation, consent, and how to request changes. Electronic consent was recorded on 06/16/2025. The clinician will provide picture choices at the next visit. The coordinator will obtain the hearing report and confirm transportation access.

IFSP REVIEW / Revisión del IFSP
North Carolina Infant-Toddler Services — FICTIONAL TEST RECORD

S:

Family information / Información familiar: Client Nicolás Arenval, preferred name Nico; DOB 06/03/2024; age 2;4. Review date 10/08/2026. Home: 184 Lantern Finch Lane, Meadowbend, NC 27900. Child ID ITP-62084; Medicaid ID 483920761Q. Parents/legal guardians: mother Elena Arenval and father Tomás Arenval. Mother’s phone 919-555-0146; father’s phone 919-555-0182. Family email arenval.family@example.com. Preferred contact: text mother after 3:30 PM; Spanish voicemail acceptable. Both parents authorize bilingual service planning.

Household includes sister Luz, age 6 years, and maternal grandmother Inés Valdoro, who provides afternoon care. Dog Miga participates in familiar play routines. Spanish predominates at home; English predominates at daycare. Parents request Spanish explanations with written English summaries. No interpreter requested today; clinician provides services directly in both languages.

Service coordinator: J. Orvena, Meadowbend River CDSA, 72 Copperleaf Court, Meadowbend, NC 27900, 252-555-0138. Treating bilingual pediatric SLP: Mara Velquín, MA, CCC-SLP, employed by Two Voices Pediatric Speech. Review held at home; father joined by telephone. Family information confirmed verbally; no demographic changes reported.

Preocupaciones, family’s own words: Mother states, “Cuando quiere algo, me jala la mano. I understand him, pero afuera se frustra porque nadie sabe.” Father states, “I want him to tell us before he cries. No queremos quitarle el español.” Grandmother states, “Conmigo señala la taza, pero si espero mucho, se enoja.” Family reports recent hitting during interrupted play; brief episodes resolve with adult support. No injury reported.

Prioridades: “Primero pedir ayuda y agua; después jugar con otros niños.” Mother wants easier breakfast and daycare pickup. Father prioritizes shared book reading without pressure to repeat. Sister Luz says, “I want him to tell me which truck.” Family prefers practical coaching embedded in existing routines. No preference for English over Spanish targets; meaningful communication in either language counts.

Rutinas diarias: Wake approximately 6:45 AM; breakfast 7:15 AM. Child reaches toward yogurt, pushes away unfamiliar textures, and accepts choices when objects are visible. Daycare drop-off 8:10 AM, lunch 11:30 AM, nap 12:15 PM to 1:45 PM. Pickup 3:20 PM; grandmother supervises snack and patio play. Dinner 6:15 PM, bath 7:00 PM, books 7:30 PM, bedtime 8:00 PM. Weekend routines vary.

Other agencies/supports: Little Kite Early Learning provides weekday care; teacher Ms. Rita Belvera shares observations with permission. Meadowbend Family WIC supports nutrition access. Copperleaf Smart Start supplies bilingual books. PCP Dr. Noel Mirvena practices at Copper Fern Children’s Hospital. Father’s workplace, Pine Thread Parcelworks, permits telephone participation during breaks. Family reports no current DSS involvement. Program information URL: https://meadowbend-cdsa.example.com/familias.

O:

Session start 9:05 AM; stop 10:00 AM. Direct SLP intervention 9:05 AM–9:50 AM; IFSP discussion 9:50 AM–10:00 AM. Present: child, mother, grandmother, SLP, and coordinator; father participated remotely during review. Home language sampling used Spanish and English without requiring translation or repeated responses. Child alert, ambulatory, and interested in vehicles.

Prior evaluation dated 09/17/2026: REEL-4 caregiver interview yielded receptive language standard score 83, expressive language standard score 74, and language ability standard score 75. Results describe performance under that interview’s conditions. English-based norms do not fully represent this bilingual child’s experience. Functional observations and caregiver reports inform planning alongside scores; no score alone determines an outcome.

Juego/comunicación: Child initiated requests by pointing, reaching, vocalizing, or using words in 8/10 arranged opportunities. Independent spoken requests occurred in 3/10 opportunities; gestures remained effective. Productions included "más", "agua", "go", "mío", and "all done". Child said "awa" for "agua" and "ka" for "car". SLP acknowledged meaning, then modeled a short expansion without correction demands.

Comprensión: Followed familiar single-step directions in context in 7/10 opportunities with min cues. Performance decreased to 4/10 when materials were unfamiliar or adult gestures were removed. Located named familiar objects in 6/8 opportunities across languages. Accepted the instruction "dame el carro" after an initial pause. Transition from trucks to snack required mod cues, a visual object cue, and caregiver proximity.

Shared engagement: Sustained reciprocal vehicle play for approximately 4 minutes. Completed 5 turn exchanges with mother when she copied his actions. During book sharing, looked between adult and picture, pointed to a dog, and produced "guau". No requirement to maintain eye contact. SLP modeled waiting, following the child’s lead, and offering choices at his response pace.

Habla: Limited sample included [w] as [w], plus /m/, /p/, and /k/ in familiar productions. No structured articulation assessment completed. Brief language sample retained SALT code [EW] for an extra-word event; coding describes the sample and does not establish impairment. Speech intelligibility varied with context; unfamiliar-listener percentage was not calculated.

Coaching: Mother practiced pause, gesture acceptance, and one-word expansion with min cues by session end. Grandmother practiced a visible choice during snack. Child selected water through pointing plus "agua". Caregivers identified waiting too long as a frustration trigger. SLP adjusted pauses to maintain successful exchanges. No coughing, choking, or wet voice observed during this snack; feeding assessment was outside today’s scope.

A:

Clinical impression / Impresión: Functional receptive-expressive language delay remains supported by converging caregiver report and observation. Working diagnosis F80.2. Spanish-English exposure is part of the child’s communication environment; bilingual exposure does not explain the observed difficulty independently. Skills vary by familiarity, partner responsiveness, and routine demands. Single-language scores require cautious interpretation.

Strengths: Intentional gestures, emerging words across languages, imitation during motivating play, and responsive caregivers. Child uses adults effectively to obtain assistance. Frustration increases when an adult anticipates repetition or withholds a desired item after a clear request. Accepting gestures and approximations improved participation today. No evidence today supports requiring spoken responses before meeting basic needs.

Progress since initial IFSP dated 07/09/2026: Family reports more spontaneous requests at home. Observed requesting now includes several meaningful words; previous session notes described primarily reaching and vocalization. Cross-session conditions differ, so improvement is descriptive. Generalization to daycare remains incompletely verified. Teacher report mentions emerging peer interest with classmates Teo and Amaya, but clinician has not observed that setting.

Family priorities remain appropriate for intervention in natural routines. No additional formal testing indicated solely to document this review. Continue bilingual coaching, support caregiver consistency, and obtain direct daycare observations. Consider additional assessment if progress stalls or new concerns emerge. Family agrees that participation and successful message exchange are the primary measures of change.

P:

Outcome uno — Requests during meals: By 01/08/2027, child will communicate a food, drink, help, or stopping message using a word, approximation, sign, or gesture in 8/10 opportunities across breakfast and snack for 3 consecutive days. Strategies: Place two choices within view; model "agua", "más", "help", or "ya"; pause briefly; accept the message immediately. Do not withhold water to elicit speech.

Outcome dos — Shared play: By 01/08/2027, child and a familiar partner will complete 4 reciprocal turns during trucks, blocks, or books in 4/5 opportunities, with min cues. Parents and grandmother will imitate first, add one simple action, and model "mi turno"/"your turn". Sister may join voluntarily. End or modify play when the child signals disengagement.

Outcome tres — Transitions: By 12/10/2026, child will participate in daycare cleanup and departure using a visual cue plus a communicative response in 80% of documented opportunities across 2 weeks. Response may include pointing, handing over an object, or saying "bye". Teacher will preview the transition, offer one manageable action, and allow processing time. Family will use similar cues at pickup.

Services / Fechas: Speech-language intervention, individual, home or daycare, 45 minutes weekly, start 10/15/2026, projected end 01/07/2027; provider Mara Velquín. Planned visit window 9:00 AM–9:45 AM. Billing, when applicable: CPT 92507; authorization SLP-26371. Make-up visits require family agreement. Coordinator contact monthly and as needed, beginning 10/12/2026. Next IFSP review 01/08/2027.

Coordination: With documented parental consent, coordinator will request daycare routine notes and arrange observation on 10/22/2026. Transit scheduler Ada Fenrel at Meadowbend Family Ride Service will receive only information needed for transportation after separate consent. Discussion of possible future attendance at Lantern Grove Preschool remains informational; no referral sent today. PCP hearing follow-up scheduled 11/04/2026, per mother.

Seguimiento: Caregivers will note successful messages during one chosen routine; no lengthy homework assigned. SLP will review examples, adjust cueing, and record participation by language and partner. Family received Spanish explanations of consent and review procedures. Both parents expressed agreement with these outcomes and service dates. Electronic acknowledgment pending; services follow existing authorization. Documented by M.V., bilingual pediatric SLP, on 10/08/2026 at 12:10 PM.

Infant-Toddler Program IFSP Review — North Carolina

Información familiar y equipo

This fictional review was completed on October 8, 2026 for María José Salcedo Pineda, called Pepe at home. Her birth date is March 8, 2024, and her chronological age is 2;7. The family lives at 246 Lantern Fern Lane, Apartment 3C, Brisacove, North Carolina 27863, in Pinebend County. The child record number is NCITP-26041873, and the Medicaid member number is 583027416Q. Spanish is the main home language; English is also used during childcare and neighborhood activities.

Her mother, Elena Isabel Pineda Ruiz, and father, Tomás Salcedo Mejía, participated in person. Her mother prefers calls at 919-555-0146 after 4:30 p.m. and receives written summaries at elena.pineda@example.org. Her father works for Fernlight Cabinet Works and joins visits when his shift permits. Both parents requested Spanish explanations before signing English forms. They described bilingual development as a family strength and want intervention that supports communication with relatives in both languages.

Service coordinator Nadia Solís Mercer represents Pinebend Children's Developmental Services Agency, located at 81 Willow Lantern Road, Brisacove, North Carolina 27863. Her office number is 984-555-0128. This review was written by Camila Torres Bellamy, a bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist employed by Two Rivers Pediatric Communication. The team reviewed the current IFSP, caregiver observations, visit notes, and childcare information. The family received the invented resource address https://pinebend-family.example.org/routines for a printable routine planning sheet.

Preocupaciones, prioridades y vida diaria

Her mother said, “Quiero que María José me diga qué necesita antes de llorar. Sometimes I understand, pero cuando está cansada, everything becomes pointing.” Her father added, “No queremos quitarle el español. We want her to talk with abuela and also ask for help outside.” The family ranked requesting help, joining simple play, and making mealtime choices as its first priorities. They prefer practice during familiar activities instead of homework that requires a separate table or special materials.

Her grandmother, Guadalupe Pineda Soto, called Lupita, provides care on two afternoons each week. She reported, “Conmigo canta mucho, pero las palabras salen bajito.” Her brother, Juan Andrés Salcedo Pineda, called Juanito, attends Lantern Grove Elementary School. He enjoys showing his sister picture books but sometimes answers before she can respond. The family agreed that adults will coach him to offer one choice, pause, and accept a gesture or word without correcting her.

Breakfast usually begins at 7:15 a.m.. Pepe chooses between fruit and toast by reaching, then carries her cup to the table. Her mother described this as a good moment for brief language models because everyone is nearby. Dressing is harder when the family feels rushed. During shoe routines, the child pulls an adult toward the door and may drop to the floor if help is delayed. The family wants a consistent way to request assistance while preserving her choices.

At Little Lantern Bilingual Daycare, teacher Rosa Mireles Vega reports that María José watches peers before approaching them. Classroom assistant Benicio Hart Luna notices more vocalizations during songs than during group questions. She often plays beside Jesús Emiliano Vela Cruz, called Chuy, and shares blocks with Amalia Fern Ortega. Adults will invite participation in either language and avoid requiring an English response before giving a requested object. Transitions work best with a picture and a short spoken preview.

Evening play includes feeding the family dog, Nube, rolling a ball, and pretending to cook. Her aunt, Beatriz Pineda Lozano, sometimes babysits and will use the same picture choices. Neighbor Dorian Vale Kent helps carry groceries but has no caregiving role. Her father said, “Después de cenar tenemos diez minutos tranquilos; ahí sí podemos practicar.” The family chose this short play period because it already happens naturally and does not compete with bedtime or household work.

Other supports include nutrition visits through Pinebend Family WIC Office and book access through Brisacove Early Steps Partnership. Pediatrician Dr. Irene Caswell Mora at Fern Harbor Children's Hospital documented no new caregiver-reported medical concerns in the referral dated September 22, 2026. Occupational therapist Hugo Serrano Pike will consult about seating and participation if the family requests it. The coordinator will confirm releases before sharing information. No additional referral was requested during this review.

Evaluación y comunicación actual

The evaluation dated September 30, 2026 combined play observation, caregiver interview, and selected items from the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale. Observed receptive skills clustered around the 24–27-month range, with expressive skills around the 18–21-month range. These descriptive ranges summarize sampled behaviors and do not represent a bilingual diagnostic conclusion. María José followed familiar directions more consistently when adults used gestures and the language associated with that routine. Her engagement improved when adults waited instead of repeating questions quickly.

A prior developmental report dated August 19, 2026 listed the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition, a language composite standard score of 78, and the 7th percentile. It also referenced the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales, Third Edition. Those results remain attributed to that report. The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation–3 was considered but was not administered because a representative elicited speech sample was unavailable. Speech sounds will be monitored through meaningful play across both languages.

During this review, the child independently produced "más", "agua", "mami", and "go". She used "ma"] for "más"] and "awa"] for "agua"] during snack play. A brief sample contained 12 different words and 3 spontaneous two-word combinations. Initial /k/ was inconsistent, and [w] occurred in one English word approximation. A sample annotation included [EW]. These observations describe the sample only; they do not establish a speech sound disorder or justify removing either language.

Resultados, estrategias y servicios

Outcome one: By January 8, 2027, Pepe will request help, an item, or another turn during three familiar routines using a gesture, picture, word, or word combination. Success means 8/10 opportunities across two consecutive weeks, with min cues or less. The current baseline is 3/10 opportunities with mod cues. Adults will place two choices within view, model "ayuda"] or "help"], and pause. They will respond to communication immediately, then add a short model without requiring repetition.

For this outcome, her mother will practice during breakfast, her father during evening play, and her grandmother during snack. The clinician will demonstrate one strategy, observe the caregiver try it, and ask what felt useful. La meta es comunicación funcional within the family's actual day. If waiting increases distress, the adult will shorten the pause and provide assistance. Progress notes will include the routine, language used, support provided, and whether the request happened spontaneously or after a model.

Outcome two: By January 8, 2027, María José will take at least three reciprocal turns with an adult or peer during blocks, ball play, or pretend cooking in 4/5 opportunities. Her baseline is 1/5 opportunities with mod cues. Adults will follow her interest, imitate an action, and introduce one small variation. Useful models include "mi turno"], "your turn"], and "más sopa"]. Classroom staff will arrange paired play with familiar materials and allow participation through actions as well as speech.

Outcome three: By January 8, 2027, the child will participate in dressing and departure routines by choosing an item and communicating readiness or a need for help in 80% of observed opportunities. The baseline is 30%. Adults will show a two-picture sequence and offer simple choices such as "zapatos"] and "jacket"]. Her brother can hold the pictures while an adult supports the routine. The team will measure participation rather than compliance and adjust the sequence when fatigue changes her available communication.

Speech-language services will begin on October 12, 2026 and continue through January 8, 2027, once weekly for forty-five minutes at home. One monthly visit may occur at childcare with family agreement. Services include caregiver coaching and direct interaction as needed, billed under CPT 92507 with the existing referral diagnosis ICD-10 F80.2. Authorization number SLP-261012-0472 applies to this fictional service period. The coordinator will contact the family monthly to review access, scheduling, and progress toward the agreed outcomes.

The next review is scheduled for January 8, 2027 at 10:00 a.m.. The family confirmed that the outcomes reflect its priorities. Her mother said, “Así sí, poquito cada día, en español y English cuando salga.” The clinician will provide a brief bilingual summary after each visit. The coordinator will begin transition discussions at the next contact and document family preferences. Written by Camila Torres Bellamy, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, on October 8, 2026.

Greeting: Dear Sonia and Daniel,  Purpose: This note summarizes today's visit and offers a short home practice plan.

Summary: Elena used longer English phrases during pretend cooking and readily joined Spanish conversation with familiar adults. Both languages remain welcome during play. We discussed how language exposure can affect performance and why one score cannot describe communication across settings. Please continue using the language that feels natural for each family activity. There is no need to translate every sentence or ask for repeated corrections.

Measures: Earlier records included the Rossetti, Bayley, and Peabody. Today's Goldman-Fristoe yielded standard score 84 and 14th percentile. Structured trials showed 8/10 accurate initial /k/ productions with mod cues and 80% accuracy. A sample included "I want tat", targeting "cat", and [w] for /r/. The transcript retained [EW]. Billing references were CPT 92507 and ICD-10 F80.0.

Classroom: Classmates Milo Trent and Ada Neri joined turn-taking games. Ms. Solano reported easier participation when directions included pictures.

Home: Brother Nico Varela, cousins Tessa Molina and Rafi Molina, and babysitter June Alder can model short phrases. Pet dog Biscuit provides a playful topic. Practice during snack preparation; offer a model, pause, and accept pointing or speech.

Follow-up: We will review classroom examples on November 5, 2026.  Closing: Warmly, Mara Beltrán

3 de marzo de 2025

Estimada señora Lucía Robles y estimado señor Andrés Vega:

Gracias por conversar conmigo sobre su hijo Nicolás Vega Robles. Soy Elena Cifuentes, patóloga bilingüe del habla y del lenguaje de Puentes de Palabras Pediatría, en Carolina del Norte. Les escribo para explicar lo que observamos y compartir ideas sencillas para practicar en casa.

Evaluamos a Nicolás el 03/03/2025 en Escuela Infantil Sendero de Nubes, en Loma Serena. Su maestra, la Sra. López, nos recibió en el salón de la Sra. López. También participó la asistente Rosa Beltrán. El registro anterior, del martes 4 de junio de 2024, nos ayudó a conocer sus avances.

A la edad de 4;2, su hijo disfruta conversar, mirar libros y jugar con otros niños. Durante una actividad con Eva Salcedo y Bruno Mena, pidió turnos y compartió materiales. A veces necesita ayuda para explicar una idea completa o pronunciar sonidos nuevos. Cuando habla rápido, algunas palabras resultan difíciles de entender.

En PLS-5 Spanish, obtuvo una puntuación estándar de 82 en comprensión auditiva y un percentil 12. Estos resultados describen una parte de sus habilidades; también consideramos las dos lenguas que escucha y sus oportunidades para usarlas. En una tarea de vocabulario respondió correctamente 8/10, equivalente a 80%. Para producir /k/, necesitó claves moderadas. Dijo "tiero tatito" al intentar decir "quiero gatito". En nuestra muestra anotamos [EW] para una palabra adicional.

Su hermana Inés Vega puede participar en juegos breves. Su abuela Teresa Robles puede leer cuentos y esperar unos segundos antes de ayudar. Incluso pueden hablar sobre su perro Milo: dónde está, qué hace y qué necesita. No hace falta corregir cada palabra. Repitan el modelo con calma y celebren el intento.

La coordinadora Marta Solano, de CDSA de Valle Claro, recibió el resumen del 2025-02-21. La pediatra Paula Neri, de Hospital Infantil Brisa Nueva, figura como profesional de referencia. Nuestro expediente es SLP-482731, y el número ficticio de Medicaid registrado es 731482960K. La documentación incluye CPT 92507 e ICD-10 F80.2.

Como el trabajo de su mamá en Taller Textil Horizonte cambia de horario, acordamos revisar el plan el 3/18/25, a las 4:15 p. m.. El Sr. Óscar Leal, encargado del transporte, tiene anotada la dirección 184 Calle del Lucero, Loma Serena, Carolina del Norte, 27000.

Durante esta semana, prueben cinco minutos de lectura diaria. Hagan una pregunta sencilla, esperen la respuesta y amplíen lo que su hijo diga. Si se cansa, terminen con una actividad agradable.

Pueden escribirme a elena.cifuentes@example.com, llamar al (919) 555-0146 o consultar https://example.org/puentes-pediatricos. Confirmaremos los acuerdos por escrito el 18/03/2025. Gracias por compartir sus observaciones y acompañar este proceso.

Con cariño,

Elena Cifuentes
Patóloga bilingüe del habla y del lenguaje
